context: The passage as a whole is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a legal dispute between two siblings over how an inheritance should be divided.
a woman confronting how her distance from her father shaped their relationship.
a family’s immigration, traced from the bus station in Cleveland to the house in Dearborn.
a brother’s decision to sell the family home after eleven years of keeping it up.

why.A: No dispute occurs. Amir has made a list, Nadia laughs at it, and they work through the afternoon together.
why.B: Correct — the photograph and Amir’s observation drive Nadia toward recognizing her own reticence.
why.C: The 1971 arrival is one photograph near the bottom of a shoebox, and the passage never follows it forward.
why.D: No decision about selling is made or discussed; the questions raised are about wallpaper and what to keep.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that Amir’s statement "You never asked him anything" is intended to:

choices.text: accuse Nadia of deliberately neglecting their father.
observe a pattern Nadia had not recognized in herself.
defend his own decision to remain nearby.
persuade Nadia to keep the photographs.

why.A: The text explicitly says "it was not an accusation, which was what made it land."
why.B: Correct — Amir names a pattern, and the narration signals Nadia is absorbing it rather than defending herself.
why.C: Amir never justifies his own choices in the exchange.
why.D: The photographs are the occasion for the remark, not its purpose.

context: According to the passage, Amir traveled to the house from:

choices.text: Cleveland.
Ontario.
Dearborn.
the city where Nadia lived.

why.A: Cleveland is where the father arrived in 1971.
why.B: Ontario is the location of a beach in one of the photographs.
why.C: Correct — the passage states he drove ninety minutes from Dearborn every other Sunday.
why.D: Nadia’s city is never specified.

context: The detail that the house "had simply gone on being itself" primarily serves to:

choices.text: emphasize the contrast between the house’s constancy and Nadia’s own transformation.
suggest the house has stayed as it was because Amir kept it up for eleven years.
establish that the family never had the money to put the house right.
foreshadow the photograph Nadia will find at the bottom of the shoebox.

why.A: Correct — the sentence directly juxtaposes "She had changed enormously" with the unchanged house.
why.B: Amir’s storm windows and arguments about the roof come a paragraph later and are not what this line is doing.
why.C: Finances are never raised about the house. The crooked step and the cold gap are offered as continuity, not as poverty.
why.D: Nothing in the image of the unchanged house points toward the photograph or the bus station.

context: As it is used in the fifth paragraph, "administrative" most nearly means:

choices.text: having to do with government.
practical and task-oriented.
carrying authority over others.
reluctant and unwilling.

why.A: No government context is present. The paragraph is about wallpaper, boxes and what to keep.
why.B: Correct — the following sentence lists wallpaper, boxes, and decisions about what to keep.
why.C: Nadia is not asserting authority over anyone; she is cataloguing tasks in an entryway.
why.D: Her alertness is described as arriving readily, not as something resisted.

context: The statement that "the arithmetic of it had never balanced" most strongly suggests that:

choices.text: Nadia had failed to contribute her share of what the house and their father cost.
the siblings had contributed to their father’s care in unequal and incomparable ways.
Amir had been quietly resentful across the eleven years of driving out.
their father had divided what he left between them unfairly.

why.A: She sent money and called on birthdays. The imbalance the sentence names is not a financial shortfall.
why.B: Correct — the sentence follows a list contrasting Amir’s presence with Nadia’s money and birthday calls.
why.C: The passage says neither of them ever said so, and it is explicit that his remark is not an accusation.
why.D: The division of the estate is never mentioned; the sentence is about what each of them gave, not what they got.

context: In the photograph Nadia discovers, her father is described as:

choices.text: smiling nervously beside a bus at the station.
wearing an oversized coat and gripping a suitcase.
standing with her mother on a beach in Ontario.
holding a schedule board he cannot read.

why.A: The passage says outright that he was not smiling; the narrator reads him as terrified.
why.B: Correct — "a coat too large for him" and "holding a suitcase with both hands."
why.C: That describes a different photograph from the same shoebox, among the unremarkable ones.
why.D: The schedule board is behind him and too blurred to read; what he holds is the suitcase.

context: The final paragraph, describing the maple tree, primarily functions to:

choices.text: indicate that the property has become valuable in the decades since the family arrived in Dearborn.
suggest the passage of time and growth that occurred while Nadia was not paying attention.
explain why the house has always been difficult to keep warm in winter.
introduce a new conflict between the siblings for the story to resolve.

why.A: Property value is never at issue, and the tree is remembered rather than appraised.
why.B: Correct — the tree Nadia "suddenly remembered" as a stick now shades the whole west side, mirroring the years she missed.
why.C: The cold under the kitchen door is a separate detail from the opening paragraph, and shade is not cold.
why.D: The passage ends on Nadia not answering and on the light going, with no new conflict raised.

context: The passage draws a contrast between Nadia and Amir chiefly in terms of:

choices.text: the financial circumstances each of them was in.
how much affection each of them felt for their father.
the form their care took — presence versus provision.
what each of them remembers of their childhood in the house.

why.A: Money appears only as one of the things Nadia sent, never as a comparison of what either could afford.
why.B: The passage never suggests either loved him less; Amir’s point is about what neither of them could ask.
why.C: Correct — Amir drove out every other Sunday and sat through silences; Nadia sent money and fixed things.
why.D: Their childhood memories are never set against each other. Only Nadia’s are given, and only in passing.

context: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: Marchetti’s constant has been disproven by commuting data showing the average trip lengthening since 1980.
a disputed regularity in travel time reframes planning around access.
the fifteen-minute city is the only workable model for modern development, whatever its critics say about affordability.
building highways is the most effective way to reduce congestion, since new lane miles relieve the trips already being made.

why.A: The drift from twenty-two minutes to nearly twenty-seven is in the passage, but it is offered as a criticism and the passage calls the question unresolved.
why.B: Correct — the passage surveys the claim, the objections, and concludes its value lies in reframing planning.
why.C: The passage treats the affordability objection as legitimate and never claims the model is the only workable one.
why.D: The passage argues the opposite: vehicle miles rose almost exactly in proportion to lane miles, leaving congestion unchanged.

context: According to the passage, Marchetti proposed that people tolerate a daily travel time of about:

choices.text: fifteen minutes.
thirty minutes.
one hour.
ninety minutes.

why.A: Fifteen minutes refers to the later urban design concept, not Marchetti’s figure.
why.B: Thirty minutes is each way, not the daily total.
why.C: Correct — "roughly one hour of travel per day — about thirty minutes each way."
why.D: Ninety minutes is cited as an extreme in the range of U.S. commutes.

context: The examples of medieval walking villages and nineteenth-century streetcar suburbs primarily serve to:

choices.text: demonstrate that cities were healthier before the automobile arrived to spread them out.
illustrate that faster travel buys distance, not saved time.
argue that streetcars should be reintroduced along the old radial lines.
establish the chronology of European urban development from the medieval period onward.

why.A: Health is never discussed. Both examples are about radius, not about how it felt to live inside one.
why.B: Correct — both examples show settlements expanding to a new radius that still takes about thirty minutes to cross.
why.C: No policy recommendation about streetcars is made; they are cited as a stage in the same pattern.
why.D: Chronology is incidental. The three eras are offered because each repeats the same half hour.

context: The passage suggests that the observation "what looks like a stable preference may in some cases be a stable constraint" implies that:

choices.text: some long commutes reflect limited housing options rather than willing choice.
commuters consistently underestimate how long their own daily trips actually take.
the travel surveys the claim rests on are generally unreliable.
people prefer rather longer commutes than Marchetti assumed they would.

why.A: Correct — the preceding sentence describes commuters "priced out of the neighborhoods near their jobs."
why.B: Estimation error is never raised. The objection is about which populations the data cover.
why.C: The critique concerns whose choices the data capture, not whether the surveys measure accurately.
why.D: The point is the reverse: some travel farther than they would prefer, because they were priced out.

context: The 2011 study of American metropolitan areas is cited as evidence that:

choices.text: average one-way commute times rose from about twenty-two minutes in 1980 to nearly twenty-seven by 2019.
new lane capacity is absorbed within a few years by additional driving, leaving overall congestion very largely unchanged.
investment in transit delivers more accessibility per dollar than the same money spent on highway lane miles.
remote work has reduced total vehicle miles traveled across American metropolitan areas.

why.A: Those figures are real but belong to the paragraph on Marchetti’s critics, not to the 2011 study.
why.B: Correct — vehicle miles traveled rose "almost exactly in proportion to new lane miles built."
why.C: The passage never compares the two kinds of investment. The study counts lane miles and vehicle miles and nothing else.
why.D: Remote work appears only in the final paragraph, two decades after the study, and the passage calls its early data ambiguous.

context: As used in the fifth paragraph, "accessibility" most nearly means:

choices.text: the accommodations made for people with disabilities.
how much a person can reach within a given travel time.
the affordability of housing built close to transit stops.
the ease with which a driver’s licence can be obtained.

why.A: A common meaning of the word, but not the planning sense the paragraph defines.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph defines it as what people "can reach within the time they are already willing to spend."
why.C: Affordability appears later as a criticism of the fifteen-minute city, not as this definition.
why.D: Nothing in the passage concerns licensing; the paragraph is about what a trip can reach.

context: The passage characterizes the fifteen-minute city as "Marchetti’s inverted" because it:

choices.text: rejects the premise that a household’s daily travel time is stable enough to plan around.
takes the travel budget as fixed and asks what fits inside it.
aims to shrink the daily travel budget well below the half hour Marchetti identified as customary.
applies only to dense European cores, where the walking distances the model assumes already exist.

why.A: The model relies on that stability rather than rejecting it — a fixed budget is what there is to invert.
why.B: Correct — the final sentence of that paragraph states this contrast explicitly.
why.C: The model concerns how much can be reached inside the budget, and the passage says it changes nobody’s travel time at all.
why.D: The passage raises that as an open question about how far the model travels, not as part of what the model is.

context: The author’s attitude toward Marchetti’s constant is best described as:

choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of it as a genuine law of human behaviour.
qualified interest in its usefulness despite unresolved objections.
dismissal of it as a hypothesis the data have outdated.
indifference to the debate that has grown up around it.

why.A: The author writes that not everyone accepts it and calls the question unresolved.
why.B: Correct — the author presents criticisms fairly while arguing its "practical value does not depend on its being a law."
why.C: The author explicitly defends its usefulness, which does not depend on its being a law.
why.D: The passage sets out the criticisms at length before answering them, which is not indifference.

context: The passage indicates that early data on remote work are ambiguous because some remote workers have:

choices.text: returned to full-time office schedules and longer commutes.
moved farther away and now travel longer on office days, keeping weekly totals similar.
relocated into the dense fifteen-minute neighbourhoods the passage described earlier.
stopped commuting entirely once remote work arrived.

why.A: A return to full-time office work is not described; the workers in question still go in some days.
why.B: Correct — the final paragraph states exactly this pattern.
why.C: No such relocation is reported. They moved farther out, not closer in.
why.D: The passage describes them as still travelling on the days they go in, which is the whole ambiguity.

context: The main purpose of Passage A is to:

choices.text: argue that restoration is a rescue, not an option.
catalogue the chemical processes by which nitrate and acetate stock decay over time.
criticise the audiences who would rather see a print with its scars left on it.
propose new public funding for the archives doing this work.

why.A: Correct — the archivist frames decay as an arithmetic certainty and restoration as rescue, while conceding that judgment is involved.
why.B: Decay opens the passage but serves the argument for rescue rather than being the point of it.
why.C: The author expresses "some sympathy" for that objection before answering it.
why.D: Funding is never mentioned. What the passage asks for is raw scans kept beside graded versions.

context: According to Passage A, a scratch inflicted by a projectionist in 1958 should be regarded as:

choices.text: part of the film’s historical texture, and therefore something that must be preserved.
damage that is not part of the film’s own history and so may properly be removed by a restorer.
evidence of how widely the film was projected.
impossible to remove with the software now available.

why.A: The author rejects this directly: the scratches are the absence of history rather than history.
why.B: Correct — "A tear introduced by a careless projectionist in 1958 tells us about that projectionist, not about the film."
why.C: Popularity is never invoked. The projectionist tells us about the projectionist.
why.D: The passage describes removing exactly such damage from the second reel of a 1927 comedy.

context: The author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A’s claim that restorations should be "documented, reversible, and modest" by:

choices.text: rejecting it as insufficient, on the grounds that restoration ought to be halted entirely.
agreeing with it and noting that such documentation rarely reaches ordinary viewers.
dismissing it as irrelevant to the questions of grain and colour B actually raises.
arguing that archives ought not to keep the raw scans at all.

why.A: Passage B states plainly, "I do not want restoration halted."
why.B: Correct — B’s central complaint is that judgments "arrive invisibly" to streaming viewers, and asks only that they be labeled.
why.C: Documentation is precisely B’s remedy for the grain and colour problems, not something beside them.
why.D: B never opposes preserving raw scans; the complaint is that viewers never learn what was done.

context: Passage B objects to aggressive noise reduction primarily because it:

choices.text: makes a film considerably more expensive to restore than it needs to be.
strips the grain that is the physical substrate of the image.
introduces new scratches and visible artefacts into the scanned image.
cannot be applied consistently from one reel of a film to the next, so the texture shifts mid-picture.

why.A: Cost is never discussed in either passage.
why.B: Correct — B calls grain "the physical substrate of the image" and the smoothed result "technically sharper and historically falser."
why.C: Noise reduction removes rather than adds; the objection is to what it takes away.
why.D: Consistency is not the objection. B objects that the smoothed result is historically false everywhere it is applied.

context: Both passages agree that:

choices.text: restoration always involves judgment.
grain should be preserved at whatever the cost.
streaming platforms have improved access to film history.
no single original version of a color film exists.

why.A: Correct — A concedes "restoration involves judgment," and B’s entire argument concerns the invisibility of those judgments.
why.B: Only B makes grain central; A does not address it.
why.C: B treats streaming as part of the problem; A does not discuss it.
why.D: Only B makes this claim about Technicolor prints.

context: The chief difference between the two passages is that Passage A emphasizes ____, while Passage B emphasizes ____.

choices.text: the urgency of physical decay ... the invisibility of restorers’ interpretive choices
the rising cost of restoration work ... the aesthetics of photographic grain
the history of nitrate and acetate film ... the economics of streaming platforms
what audiences would prefer to see ... the techniques archives use

why.A: Correct — A opens with "Every film print is dying"; B’s stated concern is that judgments "arrive invisibly."
why.B: Neither passage discusses cost, and grain is B’s example rather than B’s subject.
why.C: Streaming appears in B only as where viewers meet an unlabelled restoration, and its economics are never analysed.
why.D: This reverses both emphases: A argues from the material and B from what the viewer is not told.

context: As used in the final paragraph of Passage B, "settle for" most nearly means:

choices.text: pay compensation for.
be satisfied with.
resolve a dispute about.
establish residence in.

why.A: Nothing in the paragraph involves money, and no compensation is offered.
why.B: Correct — the author says he would accept less than the archivist expects: labeling rather than halting.
why.C: "Settle" alone can mean this, but "settle for" does not.
why.D: The sentence is about accepting a lesser measure, not about moving anywhere.

context: The reference to restorations that were "quietly revised after this criticism" serves to:

choices.text: suggest that the concern about noise reduction is shared within the profession.
accuse restorers of having concealed their methods deliberately.
demonstrate that digital restoration is technically unreliable at high resolutions.
introduce the discussion of Technicolor prints that follows.

why.A: Correct — B notes it "suggests the concern is not merely nostalgic," citing professional revision as evidence.
why.B: "Quietly" indicates a low profile rather than deliberate concealment; B’s complaint is about what reaches viewers.
why.C: The point concerns aesthetic judgment rather than technical failure — the revised restorations worked as intended.
why.D: Technicolor is introduced in the next paragraph by its own transition, "Consider color."

context: It can be inferred that the author of Passage A includes the concession about judgment in order to:

choices.text: abandon the argument for restoration he has been making.
strengthen the argument by acknowledging the limits of his own judgment before rejecting the alternative as worse.
agree with the critics that restoration ought to be delayed until the judgments are better understood.
explain why colour timing cannot be done reliably.

why.A: The paragraph ends by rejecting inaction, which the author says preserves nothing at all.
why.B: Correct — this is a classic concession that builds credibility before the final rebuttal.
why.C: A argues that every year of delay costs frames that cannot be recovered.
why.D: A treats colour timing as an interpretation to be documented, not as something impossible.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: explaining how hydrophone networks are built and how the recordings they gather are sorted.
describing the shared, changing nature of humpback song and the competing explanations for it.
arguing that humpback song amounts to a language comparable to human speech.
documenting the decline of humpback populations across the South Pacific.

why.A: Hydrophones and the machine-learning classifiers occupy one paragraph, as the method that made the rest observable.
why.B: Correct — the passage establishes the shared-and-shifting song, then surveys three hypotheses.
why.C: The passage compares song to culture and to fashion, and never to language.
why.D: Population decline is never mentioned; what moves eastward across the Pacific is the song, not a loss.

context: According to the passage, humpback song was first described by researchers in:

choices.text: the 1950s.

why.A: Correct — "since Roger and Katy Payne first described humpback song in 1971."
why.B: That year belongs to the Marchetti paper in a different passage.
why.C: 1996 is when the novel song arrived off eastern Australia.
why.D: The passage gives no 1950s date; the earliest year it names is 1971.

context: The 1996 event off eastern Australia is significant because the local population:

choices.text: gradually modified its own existing song across several breeding seasons.
abandoned its own song and adopted a distinct song from a distant population.
stopped singing entirely for the two years that followed.
split into two groups singing two different songs.

why.A: That describes the ordinary within-season drift of the second paragraph, not what happened in 1996.
why.B: Correct — within two years the eastern population "adopted the western one wholesale."
why.C: Singing did not stop. Within two years the population was singing the western song instead.
why.D: No split is described. The passage says the replacement was adopted wholesale, by every male.

context: The passage suggests that a simple "advertisement of male quality" explanation is problematic because:

choices.text: females have not been observed responding to song.
a signal identical across all competitors cannot distinguish among individuals.
only the older males in a population sing.
song occurs primarily on the feeding grounds rather than on the breeding grounds.

why.A: Female response is not the stated objection.
why.B: Correct — the passage states that such a signal "conveys nothing about any individual."
why.C: Age is never discussed. What the passage notes is that only males sing, and that they converge.
why.D: The passage says males sing chiefly on the breeding grounds, which is what points toward mating in the first place.

context: The "novelty" hypothesis described in the passage would explain:

choices.text: why it is only the males of the species that sing.
why the song changes and spreads so fast.
why the songs travel from east to west across the Pacific.
why the complexity of a song decreases over successive seasons.

why.A: The hypothesis concerns female preference for new variants and says nothing about which sex sings.
why.B: Correct — the passage says it "would explain both the constant change and the rapid adoption."
why.C: The documented direction is the reverse: songs originate in the west and move eastward in waves.
why.D: The passage reports complexity increasing after adoption, until a new song arrives and the cycle restarts.

context: The final sentence’s comparison of whale song to "the behavior of a fashion" primarily functions to:

choices.text: argue that whales are imitating a pattern they have picked up from human culture.
characterize the observed cycle of elaboration followed by wholesale replacement.
dismiss the scientific significance of the complexity finding.
introduce a fourth hypothesis, this one about female choice.

why.A: No claim of imitation is made. The resemblance is the author’s analogy, not a route of influence.
why.B: Correct — the sentence follows the finding that songs grow elaborate, then are replaced when a new one arrives.
why.C: The author introduces that finding as one that "complicates the picture usefully."
why.D: It offers an analogy for a pattern already described rather than a further explanation of it.

context: As used in the passage, "propagate" most nearly means:

choices.text: reproduce biologically.
spread through the population.
become louder.
be recorded.

why.A: A common meaning of the word, but the sentence concerns song changes, not breeding.
why.B: Correct — the next sentence explains that every male adopts the changes within weeks.
why.C: The passage never mentions how loud the song is, only how widely it spreads.
why.D: Recording is a research method described later.

context: It can be inferred that passive acoustic monitoring is valuable to researchers chiefly because it:

choices.text: allows song to be tracked across ocean basins without disturbing the animals.
produces recordings of markedly higher quality than earlier methods managed.
makes it possible to identify individual whales one by one.
removes the need for machine-learning analysis of the recordings.

why.A: Correct — the passage notes whales "cannot be marked without considerable disturbance" and that hydrophones track songs "without observing the singers at all."
why.B: Recording quality is never compared. What the passage contrasts is continuous coverage against years of manual analysis.
why.C: The passage says individuals cannot be marked without considerable disturbance, and hydrophones never see the singers.
why.D: Machine learning is described as doing the sorting that monitoring made necessary, not as something it replaced.

context: The "population marker" hypothesis differs from the "coordination" hypothesis in that only the former:

choices.text: assigns the song a role in identifying members of the same breeding group.
assumes that females play no part at all in selecting which male to mate with.
accounts for the changes the song undergoes each year.
rests on data gathered by acoustic monitoring.

why.A: Correct — the population-marker hypothesis is defined by conspecific identification; the coordination hypothesis concerns spacing and readiness among males.
why.B: Both hypotheses de-emphasise direct female attraction, so that is not what separates them.
why.C: Neither is offered as an explanation of annual change; that is the work the novelty hypothesis does.
why.D: Monitoring is the method behind all of the research described, so it cannot distinguish one hypothesis from another.

context: The passage is best described as an account of:

choices.text: a bank’s decision to stop lending to a business it had carried for years.
a narrator coming to understand why the mother’s finances were never only financial.
a family’s decision to sell the bakery once the winter losses became clear.
the economic history of a coastal town as the tourist season came to dominate it.

why.A: Mr. Callan grants the loan again in the year the narrator attends, and walks them to the door afterward.
why.B: Correct — the narrator moves from criticizing the arithmetic to grasping what the mother was also counting.
why.C: No sale is discussed. The question in the passage is whether the door stays open, not who owns it.
why.D: The town is the setting. The eleven families and the fishing crews are given as what the mother counted, not as a history.

context: According to the passage, the narrator was how old when accompanying the mother to the bank?

choices.text: Fifteen
Nineteen
Twenty-three
Thirty-nine

why.A: The age at which the narrator was first right about the arithmetic.
why.B: Correct — "when I was nineteen and had opinions."
why.C: Twenty-three is not a number the passage attaches to the narrator at all.
why.D: Not stated; roughly twenty years have passed since.

context: The detail that Mr. Callan asks after a grandmother who has been dead six years most strongly suggests that:

choices.text: he has not been told that the grandmother died six years earlier.
the exchange is a ritual whose purpose is connection rather than information.
the mother is deceiving him about her circumstances to secure the loan.
he is close to retirement and no longer following the details.

why.A: The narrator says outright that Callan knew she was dead, which is what makes the question a ritual.
why.B: Correct — the passage calls it "part of it too," and the closing paragraph names it as one of the other things being counted.
why.C: The deception reading is closed off by the phrase "a woman he knew was dead" — both of them know.
why.D: Nothing indicates his career stage, and he is attentive enough to remember her long division from school.

context: The sentence "She listened to all of it without interrupting, which should have warned me" primarily serves to:

choices.text: show that the mother agreed with the arithmetic her son had just laid out.
signal, in hindsight, that the mother had a reply the narrator had not anticipated.
establish that the mother was concentrating on the forty-minute drive inland.
introduce a conflict that permanently divides the narrator and the mother.

why.A: She does agree with the arithmetic, and says so later — but agreement is not what the narrator was warned of.
why.B: Correct — "should have warned me" is retrospective narration flagging what follows.
why.C: No distraction is described, and she answers the argument in full on the way back.
why.D: No rupture occurs. The narrator spends twenty years working out what she meant.

context: As used in the passage, "counting" most nearly means:

choices.text: reciting a series of numbers aloud.
taking into account as part of the decision.
depending on another person for help when it is needed.
expecting a particular outcome to arrive.

why.A: No literal counting occurs anywhere in the passage; the mother is weighing, not reciting.
why.B: Correct — the mother weighs non-financial factors alongside the arithmetic.
why.C: That is the sense of "counting on", and the passage has her counting things rather than counting on anyone.
why.D: "Counting on" an outcome means expecting it, but there is no "on" here — she is counting other things.

context: The passage indicates that the bakery sold bread at a loss during the winter because:

choices.text: the flour supplier raised prices once the tourist season ended.
closing for the winter would have meant not reopening in summer.
the fishing crews could not afford to pay the summer prices.
a competitor had opened nearby and taken the winter trade.

why.A: Supply costs are never mentioned. The loss comes from selling to a town that has emptied.
why.B: Correct — "if she closed the door in November it would not open in June."
why.C: No difficulty over payment is described; the crews are named as part of what the bakery was for.
why.D: No competitor appears. Mr. Callan’s remark assumes the bakery is the only such place in town.

context: Mr. Callan’s remark about February is directed at the narrator rather than the mother most likely because:

choices.text: the mother had asked him to explain the loan to her son on the way out.
he recognized that the narrator was the one who needed the reason spelled out.
he was avoiding the mother’s eye after granting the loan again.
the narrator had asked him directly why the bank kept lending.

why.A: No such request is described. She lets the narrator sit with it for ten miles instead.
why.B: Correct — the narrator has just argued the arithmetic is insane, and Callan supplies the counting the narrator is missing.
why.C: No such detail appears, and he has just come out from behind his desk to see them off.
why.D: The narrator says nothing at the bank and only shakes his hand.

context: The narrator at nineteen differs from the narrator telling the story chiefly in:

choices.text: understanding what the mother was weighing beyond profit.
ability to perform the arithmetic the bakery’s finances required.
affection for the mother and for what she was doing.
knowledge of the town and the eleven families in it.

why.A: Correct — the closing paragraph describes twenty years of working out what she meant.
why.B: The arithmetic was right at nineteen and is still right; the mother concedes it twice.
why.C: No change in affection is indicated — the narrator went with her and has thought about her answer for twenty years.
why.D: The town is equally familiar to the narrator at both ages; what changes is what the narrator counts.

context: The final sentence functions primarily to:

choices.text: concede that the mother’s way of running the bakery could not have lasted another decade.
reverse the narrator’s earlier framing by making the human factors the point of the ledger.
explain how the spring loan was eventually repaid out of summer trade.
introduce a character who had not appeared in the story before.

why.A: The narrator never retracts the arithmetic, but conceding it is not what the final sentence does.
why.B: Correct — it states that these factors were "the actual reason the ledger existed," not additions to it.
why.C: Repayment is never resolved. The passage says the summer profit never quite closed the gap.
why.D: No new character appears; the grandmother, Callan and the families are all already there.

context: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: Elisha Gray deserves as much credit for the telephone as Bell received.
simultaneous invention is common, which complicates how societies reward invention.
patents should be abolished and replaced with prizes across every industry.
individual brilliance plays no real role in how technology advances.

why.A: Gray opens the passage as the illustration of a pattern, and the passage never argues about who deserves the credit.
why.B: Correct — the passage documents the pattern and then traces its implications for patents.
why.C: The passage reports that argument from some economists and then answers it, concluding only that one uniform regime is unlikely to suit all sectors.
why.D: It says the opposite in as many words: this view does not deny individual brilliance, it relocates it.

context: Ogburn and Thomas catalogued how many cases of simultaneous invention?

why.A: 48 is 148 with the leading digit dropped. Detail questions reward going back to the sentence instead of trusting a half-remembered number.
why.B: No such figure appears. 118 is near enough to 148 to feel familiar, which is exactly why the sentence has to be reread.
why.C: Correct — the passage states 148 cases.
why.D: This is the year Bell filed his patent.

context: The mention of Helmholtz and the telegraph industry serves primarily to:

choices.text: prove that Bell took his design from work already published.
name what made the telephone solvable.
explain the procedure by which a patent and a caveat are filed.
compare European research with the American work that followed it.

why.A: No plagiarism is alleged. Bell is called a gifted experimenter working a genuinely hard problem.
why.B: Correct — they are given as the prerequisites that put Bell in "a room that many people had entered."
why.C: Filing procedure is never described, and the distinction between Bell’s patent and Gray’s caveat is not explained.
why.D: No such comparison is drawn. Helmholtz is named as a prerequisite, not as one side of a contest.

context: It can be inferred that a defender of the patent system would most likely respond to the simultaneity argument by claiming that:

choices.text: simultaneous invention has never really occurred at all.
the prospect of a monopoly is what drives the costly final effort.
inventions are entirely determined by the conditions already in place.
prizes are always a better instrument than patents.

why.A: The passage treats the pattern as well documented, with 148 catalogued cases.
why.B: Correct — the passage attributes exactly this reply to patent defenders.
why.C: That is the argument a patent defender is resisting, not one they would make.
why.D: That is the opposing position, which the passage attributes to some economists.

context: According to the passage, studies of pharmaceuticals suggest that:

choices.text: weak patent protection still produced a substantial amount of innovation in that sector.
strong patent protection matters where development costs are high and copying is easy.
patents have no effect on innovation that can be measured.
prizes work better than patents at encouraging new drugs.

why.A: That is the finding from the nineteenth-century industrial exhibitions, which the passage sets against the drug studies.
why.B: Correct — the passage says pharmaceutical studies "find the opposite."
why.C: The passage reports a real effect in that sector, which is why it calls the overall evidence mixed.
why.D: Prizes are raised as a proposal by some economists, and no pharmaceutical comparison of the two is reported.

context: As used in the passage, "relocates" most nearly means:

choices.text: moves something to a new physical address.
reassigns to a different place in the explanation.
does away with something entirely.
measures something precisely.

why.A: No physical movement is described; what moves is where brilliance sits in the explanation.
why.B: Correct — brilliance is repositioned within a causal account rather than removed.
why.C: The sentence says explicitly that this view does not deny brilliance, so nothing is eliminated.
why.D: Nothing is being measured. The verb governs brilliance, which the passage treats as real but repositioned.

context: The passage suggests that a patent monopoly may "retard the very diffusion it was designed to encourage" because it:

choices.text: restricts use of a solution that others would have reached anyway.
requires an inventor to publish the whole of the method in full.
lasts for too short a period to matter.
applies only to the pharmaceutical industry.

why.A: Correct — if timing rather than creation is rewarded, the monopoly blocks others who were nearly there.
why.B: Publication would spread a solution rather than hold it back, so it cannot be the reason diffusion slows.
why.C: Duration is never discussed, and a shorter monopoly would slow diffusion less, not more.
why.D: Pharmaceuticals are one example among several, and the passage’s point is that the answer varies by industry.

context: The final paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: propose a specific reform for the patent system to adopt.
explain why the inaccurate story survives despite the evidence.
summarise the exhibition studies and the pharmaceutical ones.
introduce one more case of simultaneous invention.

why.A: No reform is proposed there; the proposals appear two paragraphs earlier and are left unresolved.
why.B: Correct — it argues the lone-inventor story persists because it is useful, not because it is true.
why.C: The studies are not revisited. The paragraph turns from evidence to why the story survives it.
why.D: No new case appears; the paragraph is about what the pattern costs a storyteller.

context: The passage contrasts the popular telling of the Bell–Gray story with the historians’ telling chiefly in that historians treat the coincidence as:

choices.text: evidence of fraud by one of the two.
typical rather than exceptional.
a legal dispute between two claimants.
an unimportant detail of the record.

why.A: Fraud is never suggested; Gray filed a caveat on the same day and the passage treats both as independent.
why.B: Correct — "the simultaneity is not the anomaly. It is the pattern."
why.C: The patent conflict is background. What interests historians is that two people arrived at once.
why.D: They treat it as highly significant — the simultaneity is the pattern rather than the anomaly.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: the medical treatment available for focal dystonia and why so little of it works.
how relearning an instrument after injury changed the author’s understanding of playing.
arguing that musicians would be better off practising far fewer hours a day.
the author’s early successes as a violinist before the injury.

why.A: The passage says in one clause that there is almost no useful treatment, and never returns to the subject.
why.B: Correct — the arc runs from loss to relearning to a different kind of understanding.
why.C: The ninety-minute limit is a constraint the author was under, offered as autobiography rather than advice.
why.D: Early success occupies the opening sentence, which exists to set up the loss in the same breath.

context: According to the passage, focal dystonia is:

choices.text: painful but largely treatable with rest.
painless but disabling.
caused by a single injury to a tendon in the hand.
reversible with enough rest from playing.

why.A: The passage says it is painless and that there is almost no useful treatment.
why.B: Correct — "It is painless. It is also, for a musician, absolute."
why.C: It is described as neurological — the brain’s map of the hand degrading — rather than as tendon damage.
why.D: No reversal is described. The author rebuilt the skill on the other side instead.

context: The author found the neurologist’s explanation "clarifying" most likely because it:

choices.text: offered a course of treatment that might reverse the damage.
identified sameness of movement as the cause, which suggested how to practice differently.
showed that the injury had not been the author’s own fault after all.
showed that the condition is common among violinists who practise for as many hours.

why.A: No cure is offered anywhere in the passage; the author calls the condition, for a musician, absolute.
why.B: Correct — the author later says "sameness was now the enemy" and varies everything.
why.C: The explanation implicates the author’s own practice, and blame is never what the passage is weighing.
why.D: Prevalence is never mentioned. What the explanation gives the author is a cause, not company.

context: The author’s second period of learning differed from the first in that it relied on:

choices.text: imitation, scales and long daily hours.
analysis, variation, and limited practice time.
a different teacher and a different method.
a smaller instrument suited to the other hand.

why.A: That is the first learning, at nine: imitation and volume, with hours, scales and correction.
why.B: Correct — the author worked out motions in advance, varied everything, and practiced ninety minutes a day.
why.C: No teacher is mentioned in either period. The method changed because the author worked it out alone.
why.D: The instrument was restrung in reverse, not resized; nothing about its dimensions changed.

context: As used in the passage, "absolute" most nearly means:

choices.text: flawless in every respect.
total.
certain to be diagnosed.
unrelated to other conditions.

why.A: Nothing is being praised as perfect.
why.B: Correct — for a musician the condition is complete in its consequences despite being painless.
why.C: Diagnosis is not the subject of the sentence.
why.D: No comparison to other conditions is made.

context: The comparison of the lost skill to "a rented thing" primarily conveys:

choices.text: the financial cost of fourteen years of violin training.
the shock of discovering that something felt innate was contingent.
that the instrument itself had been borrowed rather than owned.
that the skill was only suspended and would eventually return.

why.A: Cost is never discussed. The word "rented" describes how securely the skill was held, not what it was paid for.
why.B: Correct — the skill had felt like a property of the body, "like being right-handed," until it was revoked.
why.C: No borrowed instrument appears; the metaphor is about the skill, which the author calls a property of the body.
why.D: It did not return. The author rebuilt it on the other side across nine years.

context: The author anticipates that the closing claim may sound like "consolation" and denies it. This suggests the author believes:

choices.text: the second learning produced a real gain, not merely a comforting story.
readers may not quite believe the injury happened the way it is described.
the technical loss turned out to be insignificant.
other musicians would gain from a similar setback.

why.A: Correct — the author insists on a form of understanding available only through rebuilding.
why.B: The injury’s reality is never in question. What the author expects to be doubted is the claim of a gain.
why.C: The author says the opposite in the same sentence: a better musician, though a technically lesser one.
why.D: The passage draws no such recommendation, and the author spent two years finding the cause unbearable.

context: The passage suggests that the first learning and the second differed most fundamentally in:

choices.text: which hand held the bow and which the strings.
whether the process was examined or taken for granted.
the kind of music the author set out to study.
how much natural talent the author had to work with.

why.A: The switch is true, and it is the occasion for the difference rather than the difference itself.
why.B: Correct — the closing states the author "could no longer take any part of it for granted."
why.C: Genre is never mentioned; the same instrument and the same repertoire are implied throughout.
why.D: Talent is never the variable. What changed is that nothing could be taken for granted.

context: How long did it take the author to reach, left-handed, a level passed at thirteen on the original side?

choices.text: Two years
Nine years
Fourteen years
Twenty-six years

why.A: The period spent finding the explanation unbearable.
why.B: Correct — "it took nine years."
why.C: The length of the original training.
why.D: The age at which relearning began.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: establishing that the accumulation of senescent cells is the single cause of age-related decline.
how understanding of cellular senescence evolved and why clearing these cells is promising but cautious.
the career of Leonard Hayflick, from the 1961 culture experiments through the telomere work that followed.
arguing that senolytic drugs are ready for use and that regulatory recognition is the only thing still missing.

why.A: The passage offers senescence as one thread and says the simple picture — cells run out, tissues decline — has since become considerably more complicated.
why.B: Correct — it traces the Hayflick limit through telomeres, the secretory phenotype, and senolytics with caveats.
why.C: Hayflick occupies one paragraph, and the telomere mechanism is not attributed to him at all.
why.D: The closing paragraph argues the opposite, naming impaired wound healing and unknown cancer risk as reasons for caution.

context: According to the passage, telomeres:

choices.text: are what allows a cell to divide indefinitely.
cap chromosomes and shorten with each division.
are produced and secreted by senescent cells.
were first identified by Alexis Carrel in culture.

why.A: Their shortening is what ends division, which is the opposite of allowing it to continue.
why.B: Correct — repetitive sequences capping chromosomes that absorb end-replication loss.
why.C: They are structures on the chromosome, not part of the secretory phenotype.
why.D: Carrel’s contaminated experiment is cited as the source of the opposite belief, that cells were immortal.

context: The passage states that senescent cells:

choices.text: die shortly after their final division rather than persisting.
stop dividing but remain alive and secrete signaling molecules.
continue dividing, but at a much slower rate than before.
appear only in elderly animals, not in young ones.

why.A: The passage is explicit that a senescent cell stops dividing permanently but does not die.
why.B: Correct — they permanently stop dividing and produce the secretory phenotype.
why.C: Division stops entirely once telomeres shorten past the threshold; it does not merely slow down.
why.D: Young animals produce them continuously. What changes with age is that removal becomes less efficient.

context: It can be inferred that researchers pursued clearing senescent cells rather than preventing senescence because prevention would:

choices.text: be technically impossible with current methods.
remove a mechanism that protects against cancer.
require the kind of genetic engineering used on the mice.
shorten telomeres faster than division already does.

why.A: The passage never says prevention cannot be done, only that it would give something up.
why.B: Correct — the passage notes senescence "is also a defense against cancer."
why.C: That engineering was a way to destroy senescent cells in mice, not a way to prevent senescence.
why.D: Preventing senescence would not shorten telomeres — telomere shortening is what triggers it.

context: The reference to Alexis Carrel’s contaminated experiment serves to:

choices.text: explain why cells were wrongly believed to be immortal before 1961.
demonstrate that senescence is also a defense against cancer.
introduce the senescence-associated secretory phenotype.
describe an early attempt at a senolytic treatment.

why.A: Correct — the belief rested "largely on a contaminated experiment."
why.B: That point arrives several paragraphs later and rests on the logic of a cell that cannot divide, not on Carrel.
why.C: The phenotype is introduced much later, and nothing about Carrel’s culture bears on it.
why.D: Senolytics were identified decades afterward, and Carrel’s experiment established nothing about clearing cells.

context: As used in the passage, "indication" most nearly means:

choices.text: a sign or hint that something is about to happen.
a medical condition a treatment is approved to address.
a reading taken from an instrument or a test.
a warning printed on a drug’s packaging.

why.A: That is the common sense of the word, but the sentence is about what regulators approve a drug to treat.
why.B: Correct — the sentence concerns regulators not recognizing aging as a treatable condition.
why.C: Nothing in the sentence is being measured; the word sits inside a regulatory phrase.
why.D: No labelling is discussed. The sentence concerns which conditions a treatment may be approved for.

context: The passage suggests that the senescence-associated secretory phenotype is best described as:

choices.text: harmful wherever it appears, at any age.
beneficial in the short term and harmful when sustained.
largely irrelevant to how an organism ages.
a consequence of telomeres lengthening past a threshold.

why.A: It recruits immune cells, aids wound healing and helps clear damaged tissue in the short term.
why.B: Correct — useful "in small numbers and for short periods," damaging when cells accumulate over years.
why.C: It is the centre of the passage’s account: the same secretions drive chronic inflammation as the cells accumulate.
why.D: Telomeres shorten past a threshold. Nothing in the passage describes them lengthening.

context: Early human trials of senolytics have targeted:

choices.text: aging itself, on the strength of the extended lifespan seen in mice.
specific diseases rather than aging itself.
the prevention of cancer in patients already at high risk.
the acceleration of wound healing after major surgery.

why.A: The passage says trials target specific conditions rather than aging, because regulators do not recognise aging as an indication.
why.B: Correct — pulmonary fibrosis and diabetic kidney disease are the named targets.
why.C: Cancer appears only as a reason for caution about clearing these cells, never as a trial target.
why.D: Wound healing is named as something indiscriminate clearing might impair, which is the opposite of a target.

context: The closing sentence, "It is how many, where, and when," primarily serves to:

choices.text: reject senolytics as unworkable, given how much about their long-term effects is still unknown.
reframe the issue from whether these cells are harmful to how precisely they must be managed.
summarise the mouse results on cardiac function, frailty and median lifespan.
call for regulators to move faster on approving senolytic treatments.

why.A: The passage reports substantial results in mice and preliminary human trials, not a dead end.
why.B: Correct — it replaces a yes/no framing with questions of dose, location, and timing.
why.C: Those results appear two paragraphs earlier, and the closing sentence does not restate them.
why.D: The paragraph it closes is the one arguing for caution, and it names two specific unknowns.

context: The example comparing "an hour of accounting advice and an hour of yard work" in the first paragraph primarily functions to—

choices.text: prove that accounting advice is objectively less valuable than yard work.
introduce the critics who argue that time banks fail to scale up to the needs of an entire neighborhood.
explain why some time banks choose to exclude licensed trades from their exchanges.
illustrate concretely what the time bank's flat, hour-for-hour equivalence actually means in practice.

why.D: This early example makes the abstract idea of flat hour-for-hour value concrete, before the passage moves on to discuss administration and critics.
why.A: The passage makes no claim about the objective value of either service.
why.B: The critics are introduced in a later paragraph, not through this example.
why.C: That explanation appears in a later paragraph and is not connected to this specific comparison.

context: The sentence "What mattered, Master Alduin often said, was that a chart carried his name" primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: prove that Master Alduin's charts were more accurate than those of his professional rivals.
explain the personal stakes that make Master Alduin resistant to being corrected.
foreshadow that Master Alduin will eventually dismiss Mireille from her apprenticeship.
provide historical background on how the shipping company was originally founded.

why.B: This sentence gives the reader Master Alduin's own stated reasoning for why he resists correction — his name and reputation are on the line — which explains both his treatment of the journeyman and Mireille's fear of confronting him.
why.A: The sentence is about his attitude toward his reputation, not a comparison to other cartographers.
why.C: The passage's ending contradicts this — he keeps her on and extends her more responsibility.
why.D: The sentence is about Master Alduin's personal values, not the shipping company's history.

context: The sentence "Understood in isolation, holding a seed hostage to fire looks like poor design. Understood against the specific ecology of a fire-adapted forest, it looks instead like the only design that reliably works" primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: summarize the passage's overall conclusion after all of its supporting evidence has been presented.
introduce a competing scientific theory that the rest of the passage will go on to refute.
signal a shift from describing serotiny's apparent costs to the ecological logic that justifies them.
prove that serotinous trees are more intelligent than non-serotinous conifer species.

why.C: This sentence pivots the passage from the apparent evolutionary gamble of serotiny to the detailed ecological explanation that occupies the remaining paragraphs.
why.A: This sentence appears early, before most of the supporting evidence, functioning as a transition rather than a final summary.
why.B: No competing theory is introduced or refuted anywhere in the passage.
why.D: The passage never makes any claim about tree intelligence.

context: The sentence "That was the whole of the job, Master Okafor liked to say. Not the flame. The turning." primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: reveal that Master Okafor considers the flame itself unimportant to the lighthouse's function.
explain why Renata was initially denied permission to stand a solo watch.
foreshadow that the lighthouse will eventually be replaced by an automated system.
establish early the mechanical detail that becomes central to the crisis later that night.

why.D: By naming the turning, rather than the flame, as the real job, this early sentence sets up the gear failure that becomes the passage's central problem.
why.A: Overstates his view — he is drawing a distinction of emphasis, not calling the flame unimportant.
why.B: Unrelated to the four-month wait mentioned in the opening sentence.
why.C: No such topic appears anywhere in the passage.

context: The comparison to a building whose 'materials...age faster than the design they were meant to serve' primarily functions in the passage to—

choices.text: argue that older translations should be physically discarded rather than kept in print.
suggest that translators need formal training in architecture to do their work well.
clarify why retranslation is maintenance rather than the correction of past mistakes.
prove that all buildings and all translations eventually fail in the same way.

why.C: This comparison directly follows the sentence stating 'retranslation is not vanity in this light; it is maintenance,' clarifying that idea with a concrete parallel.
why.A: No such argument about discarding older translations is made.
why.B: The architecture reference is a comparison, not a claim about translator training.
why.D: Overstates the comparison into a universal claim the passage never makes.

context: The description of the note app opening 'by accident...into an email I meant to answer three days ago' in Passage A primarily functions to—

choices.text: criticize a specific email application by name for its poor design.
explain why the author originally chose to give up a phone journal and start keeping a paper one instead.
give a concrete example of the kind of distraction the author believes a paper notebook eliminates.
suggest that the author has generally poor time-management skills.

why.C: This specific, embarrassing example makes concrete the paragraph's broader claim that a notebook 'cannot open, by accident, into some other application entirely.'
why.A: No specific application is named in the passage.
why.B: This detail illustrates a drawback of phone journaling, not the author's original motivation for journaling.
why.D: The detail is offered as an example of the tool's distraction, not as a broader claim about the author's habits.

context: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the passage?

choices.text: It explains how time banks work and why they appeal, then examines what separates a bank that lasts from one that folds.
It presents two opposing historical accounts of when time banking first began, then resolves the disagreement.
It narrates, in chronological order, the founding and eventual collapse of one specific time bank.
It opens with a critic's objection and spends the remainder of the passage refuting it point by point.

why.A: The passage moves from defining the time-bank concept and its motivation to analyzing the administrative and social factors that separate lasting banks from failing ones.
why.B: No competing historical origin accounts appear anywhere in the passage.
why.C: The passage discusses time banks in general terms, not the history of one specific bank.
why.D: The passage does not open with an objection, and it does not simply refute the critics it later discusses.

context: Which choice best describes the relationship between the passage's fourth and fifth paragraphs?

choices.text: The fourth paragraph presents a hypothesis, and the fifth paragraph reports an experiment that disproves it.
The two paragraphs describe two entirely unrelated adaptations found in different pine species.
The fourth paragraph is a historical account, and the fifth paragraph is a prediction about the future.
The fourth paragraph explains an advantage of synchronized germination, and the fifth a cost of it.

why.D: The fourth paragraph explains why synchronized germination benefits a new generation of seedlings, and the fifth paragraph turns to the forest-scale cost of that same synchronization.
why.A: No experiment or disproof is described in the fifth paragraph.
why.B: Both paragraphs concern the same synchronized-germination adaptation in serotinous pines.
why.C: Neither paragraph is framed as history or as a future prediction.

context: The tone of the passage's final paragraph is best described as—

choices.text: quietly admiring, treating Renata's competence as noteworthy though unremarked.
openly celebratory, matching the harbor office's enthusiastic reaction to the news.
bitterly ironic, mocking Master Okafor's inability to praise his assistant properly.
coldly clinical, focused only on the technical details of the gear replacement.

why.A: The paragraph's focus on how Renata comes to understand his understated words as a genuine compliment gives it a quietly admiring tone.
why.B: The harbor office's reaction is never described as enthusiastic.
why.C: The paragraph is sincere, not ironic or mocking.
why.D: The paragraph focuses on what his words meant to Renata, not on technical detail.

context: The tone of the passage toward the practice of retranslating classic novels is best described as—

choices.text: dismissive, treating retranslation as a wasteful publishing gimmick.
nostalgic, longing for a return to nineteenth-century translation standards.
alarmed, warning readers that most modern translations cannot be trusted.
measured, treating retranslation as a reasonable response to real change.

why.D: Across all three of its supporting reasons, the passage explains retranslation calmly and even-handedly, including a fair hearing of its critics, which gives it a measured, analytical tone.
why.A: Contradicted — the passage takes retranslation seriously as 'maintenance,' not waste.
why.B: The passage explains why earlier standards became dated rather than idealizing them.
why.C: No alarm or warning of this kind appears in the passage.

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "smooth" in the phrase "her explanation rehearsed so many times it had worn smooth" most nearly means—

choices.text: practiced until it flowed without hesitation.
physically flat and even in surface texture.
calm and even-tempered in her manner.
polished to a glossy, reflective shine.

why.A: The passage uses "worn smooth" figuratively, the way repeated handling wears an object smooth, to describe an explanation Mireille has rehearsed so many times that it comes out fluently, without stumbling.
why.B: The literal, physical meaning of "smooth," not the figurative meaning used here.
why.C: Describes a personality trait, not the rehearsed quality of an explanation.
why.D: Another literal, physical sense of the word that doesn't fit an explanation being described.

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "ledger" in the final paragraph most nearly means—

choices.text: a physical book bound in leather, used for older accounting methods.
a formal record that tracks what each member has given and is owed.
a legal contract that obligates a member to repay a debt.
a public announcement of a time bank's rules to new members.

why.B: Throughout the passage, "ledger" refers to the record system that tracks members' hours given and owed, not a physical object or a set of rules.
why.A: The literal, physical sense of the word, not how it functions in this passage's discussion.
why.C: Overstates the term — the passage treats a deficit as trust-based, not a binding legal contract.
why.D: Confuses the ledger with a set of rules, which the passage discusses separately.

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "stilted" in the fourth paragraph most nearly means—

choices.text: elevated on physical supports, as a building might be.
deliberately funny in a way that is out of place.
exceptionally rich in figurative language and imagery.
unnaturally stiff and awkward in phrasing.

why.D: The passage uses "stilted" to describe sentences produced by a translation aiming at maximum literal precision — stiff, awkward English rather than natural prose.
why.A: The literal, architectural sense of the word, not the sense used to describe prose here.
why.B: Conflates 'stilted' with 'comic,' a different quality raised elsewhere in the passage.
why.C: Close to the opposite of the word's meaning here — stilted prose reads as forced, not richly figurative.

context: As it is used in the passage, the word "cohort" in the fifth paragraph most nearly means—

choices.text: a group that shares the same age because they began life at the same time.
a small committee formed to manage a shared forest resource.
a single tree that happens to produce an unusually large number of cones.
a species of insect that feeds specifically on pine seedlings.

why.A: The passage uses "cohort" to describe the group of trees that germinated together after the same fire and therefore ages, matures, and becomes vulnerable together.
why.B: Confuses the ecological sense of the word with an administrative sense.
why.C: The term describes a group of trees, not an individual tree's cone production.
why.D: No such insect is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

context: The main function of the third paragraph is to:

choices.text: explain why a reasonable objection was raised and how evidence finally answered it.
demonstrate that the critics of the partnership theory were motivated by professional rivalry.
introduce the chemical processes that allow lichens to break down rock.
compare the growth of a lichen with the growth of a moss.

why.A: The paragraph states that the resistance 'was not unreasonable', gives the critics' two arguments, and then describes the separate-and-recombine experiments that settled the matter. Objection followed by resolving evidence is exactly its structure.
why.B: The passage explicitly calls the resistance reasonable and never assigns the critics a motive.
why.C: The acids appear in the fourth paragraph, not the third.
why.D: The moss appears in the fifth paragraph, in the account of soil formation.

context: Which choice best describes how the passage handles the claim that multiplying translations benefits readers?

choices.text: It presents the claim, then thoroughly disproves it using historical examples.
It presents the claim's reasoning, then raises a real counterobjection without settling it.
It ignores any possible objection to the claim entirely.
It attributes the claim to a single named scholar and then discredits that scholar's other work.

why.B: The fourth paragraph lays out the reasoning for multiplying translations, and the fifth paragraph raises a fair objection to it without resolving the disagreement.
why.A: The passage does not disprove the claim — it raises a counterobjection but does not declare a winner.
why.C: Directly contradicted — a specific counterobjection is discussed at length.
why.D: No named scholar is identified or discredited anywhere in the passage.

context: Which choice best describes a weakness in Passage B's argument that could be raised using evidence from Passage A?

choices.text: Passage B never mentions the author's grandmother, so its central example is unsupported.
Passage B contradicts itself by claiming that digital notes are both searchable and difficult to organize.
Passage B fails to mention that paper notebooks are less expensive than digital devices.
Passage B never addresses Passage A's claim that the effort of handwriting improves what gets written.

why.D: Passage B's strongest counterpoint concerns friction and access after writing, but it does not directly engage Passage A's separate claim that handwriting improves what gets written in the first place.
why.A: Factually incorrect — the grandmother's diary is Passage B's central example.
why.B: Passage B does not make this contradictory claim — it consistently presents digital notes as easier to organize by tag.
why.C: Cost is not a topic either passage raises, so its absence is not a weakness in Passage B's actual argument.

context: Which choice best characterizes the relationship between the personal anecdotes used in Passage A and in Passage B?

choices.text: Both passages use a family member's experience to argue against digital note-taking.
Passage A uses a family member's notebooks, while Passage B uses the author's own habit, to argue for the same conclusion about paper.
Passage A uses the author's own habit to argue for paper, while Passage B uses a family member's notebooks to argue its limits.
Neither passage relies on a personal anecdote to support its argument.

why.C: Passage A's evidence is the author's own eleven notebooks; Passage B's evidence is the grandmother's sixty years of unsorted diaries, used to make an opposing point about paper's usefulness.
why.A: Only Passage B involves a family member; Passage A discusses the author's own habit.
why.B: Both halves are swapped: the family member's notebooks are Passage B's example and the author's own habit is Passage A's. The two also argue opposite conclusions, not the same one.
why.D: Both passages clearly rely on personal anecdotes — the author's own notebooks in A, the grandmother's diary in B.

context: A reader who accepted the reasoning in both Passage A and Passage B fully would most likely conclude that—

choices.text: digital note-taking is entirely without value for personal reflection.
handwriting guarantees a permanent record that will always remain readable to any future generation.
there is no meaningful difference between the two methods once friction is set aside.
handwriting may improve individual reflections, while a digital system better preserves access.

why.D: Combining Passage A's case for handwriting's filtering effect with Passage B's case for digital access over decades produces a synthesis in which each method offers a distinct advantage.
why.A: Contradicted by Passage B's argument, which the reader is assumed to accept.
why.B: Contradicted by Passage B's account of the grandmother's largely inaccessible diary.
why.C: Both passages describe meaningful differences beyond friction, such as searchability and tagging.

context: Which piece of evidence from the passage most directly supports the claim that time banks can formalize trust that already exists rather than create it from nothing?

choices.text: An hour of teaching a neighbor bicycle repair earns exactly the same single credit as an hour of gardening does.
Some time banks exclude licensed trades such as electrical work from the services that qualify.
Banks organized among people who already saw each other survive slow patches better than online-only ones.
Large time banks sometimes attract members trying to escape rent or utility bills.

why.C: The final paragraph's comparison between community-rooted banks and sign-up-sheet banks is the passage's direct evidence that formal trust depends on trust that already existed.
why.A: Supports the flat-equivalence design of time banks, not the trust-formalization claim.
why.B: Supports a point about administrative scope, not about trust or prior relationships.
why.D: Supports the point about scaling challenges, not the trust-formalization claim.

context: Which piece of evidence from the passage most directly supports the claim that shortened fire intervals threaten serotinous forests?

choices.text: A canopy fire converts the accumulated forest-floor litter into a thin layer of mineral-rich ash.
Foresters have begun observing land that burns and then fails to regrow the same forest it burned away.
A serotinous cone's resin does not soften at ordinary summer temperatures.
Serotinous seeds fall onto exposed ground within days of a fire's passing.

why.B: The final paragraph's observation of land that burns and fails to regrow the same forest is the passage's direct, real-world evidence for the shortened-interval threat.
why.A: Supports the claim about post-fire soil conditions, not the claim about shortened fire intervals.
why.C: Supports the description of the resin threshold, not the claim about shortened fire intervals.
why.D: Supports the timing-advantage claim, not the claim about the risk from shortened intervals.

context: Both passages are primarily concerned with—

choices.text: describing the biographical details of the authors' family members.
comparing handwritten journaling with digital note-taking as reflection tools.
arguing that one specific journaling app is clearly superior to all of its competitors.
explaining the history of the notebook as a manufactured object.

why.B: Both authors compare their own experience of handwritten and digital journaling to make a broader case for one method's advantages for personal reflection.
why.A: The grandmother is mentioned only in Passage B, and only briefly, not as the main concern of either passage.
why.C: Neither passage names or promotes a specific app.
why.D: Neither passage discusses the manufacturing history of notebooks.

context: Which choice best describes a key difference between how the author of Passage A and the author of Passage B view the friction involved in handwriting?

choices.text: The author of Passage A views the friction as a minor inconvenience, while the author of Passage B views it as the primary reason to keep a journal in the first place.
Both authors agree that the friction of handwriting is the single most important factor in choosing a journaling method.
The author of Passage A dismisses the friction entirely, while the author of Passage B considers it essential.
The author of Passage A sees that friction as a filter that improves what gets written, while the author of Passage B sees it as producing shorter entries.

why.D: Passage A treats the pen's drag and the hand's cramp as the 'entire mechanism' behind paper's usefulness, while Passage B explicitly argues the same friction can produce a worse, more guarded entry.
why.A: Reverses both authors' actual positions on friction.
why.B: Passage B explicitly downplays friction as 'not obviously a virtue,' so the two authors do not agree here.
why.C: Passage A does not dismiss the friction — the author explicitly values it; this distractor swaps the two authors' views.

context: Based on both passages, the author of Passage B would most likely respond to Passage A's claim that a notebook 'is a room with one door' by arguing that—

choices.text: a single fixed location for a thought is a limitation, since most thoughts belong in several contexts.
a notebook's single location makes it more secure from accidental deletion than any digital system.
a room with one door is an accurate description of how digital note systems also function.
the comparison to a room is unfair, because notebooks do not actually resemble rooms in any way at all.

why.A: Passage B's central argument is that paper forces a single-location decision at the moment of writing, while a digital entry can be tagged to several places at once — the direct opposite of treating one location as an advantage.
why.B: Passage B never raises security or deletion risk as a concern.
why.C: Directly contradicts Passage B's central point that digital notes can live in multiple places at once.
why.D: Misreads the metaphor as a literal claim rather than engaging with the substance Passage B does address.

context: What most directly leads Renata to try oiling the gear housing rather than attempting some other repair?

choices.text: Written instructions Master Okafor had taped inside the lamp room door.
A suggestion radioed in from the harbor office during the storm.
A similar repair she had already performed by herself earlier that same night.
Her memory of Master Okafor using thinned oil on a swollen part in October.

why.D: The passage states plainly that what she had was the memory of Master Okafor's October repair with thinned oil, which she then applies to the gear.
why.A: The passage states those instructions do not cover this situation.
why.B: No radio contact occurs anywhere in the passage.
why.C: This is her first attempt at this repair; no earlier repair that night is described.

context: Based on the passage, what causes a translation choice that once sounded neutral to eventually sound archaic or unintentionally comic?

choices.text: The original novel's plot becomes less relevant to contemporary readers.
Later translators deliberately introduce comic errors in order to critique earlier versions.
The target language keeps changing over time while the translation's word choices remain fixed.
Publishers edit older translations without updating their original publication dates.

why.C: The third paragraph explains that words drift in register over time, so a translation calibrated to an earlier register can come to sound archaic or comic as the living language moves on without it.
why.A: The passage discusses language drift, not the plot's relevance.
why.B: No such deliberate critique is described in the passage.
why.D: Not mentioned anywhere in the passage.

context: What most directly causes Mireille to finally tell Master Alduin about the error, after having already decided to say nothing?

choices.text: Master Alduin's direct request that she double-check her soundings before he signed the chart.
Learning from the clerk that a ship had been lost near Cormorant Point on an improperly charted reef.
Her fear that she would be dismissed the way the journeyman had been two winters earlier.
The shipping company's deadline for delivering the finished chart.

why.B: The passage states plainly that it was the clerk's mention of the vessel lost eleven years earlier that changed Mireille's mind, giving the abstract quarter-mile error real, human stakes.
why.A: Master Alduin never makes this request in the passage.
why.C: This fear is part of why she initially says nothing, not why she changes her mind.
why.D: No deadline is mentioned as a cause of her decision.

context: Based on the passage, what most directly causes some large time banks to 'stall,' as the passage describes it?

choices.text: Members begin demanding cash payment instead of hourly credit once the bank has grown past a certain size.
The bank's administrators run out of hours to allocate to new members.
Licensed tradespeople refuse to participate once a bank exceeds a certain size.
Supply and demand for different kinds of labor fail to match, so the help a member needs is missing.

why.D: The fourth paragraph explains that a stall occurs when a bank has plenty of one kind of labor and little of another, the same way any market stalls when supply and demand fail to match.
why.A: Not described in the passage — the stall is attributed to mismatched labor supply, not a shift to cash.
