why.A: It is introduced as the reason "attempts to reproduce the bag result elsewhere have been uneven", and the passage supplies the mechanism: whether a usable alternative is already in the shopper’s possession.
why.B: That is the consistent result the passage is trying to explain, so it cannot be evidence of unevenness.
why.C: The bonus result separates the two explanations of why the charge worked. It says nothing about where charges transfer.
why.D: That is a psychological principle the passage draws on, not a finding about the reach of the policy.

context: The passage’s closing sentences suggest that a policymaker designing an incentive is most likely to go wrong by:

choices.text: assuming that a bigger number will produce a bigger effect.
setting the charge lower than the public will tolerate.
relying on evidence from a single city.
choosing a charge when a bonus would be cheaper.

why.A: The last two sentences name the error: not "setting the number too low", but "treating the number as the thing that matters" — which is the assumption that size and effect track each other.
why.B: The passage explicitly rejects this as the common error in the sentence before its conclusion.
why.C: Evidence from several jurisdictions is cited, and the unevenness of the cup results is presented as instructive rather than as a methodological warning.
why.D: Cost to the treasury is never discussed, and the bonus is reported as the weaker instrument.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a verification requirement that was poorly designed, and the unrelated change that eventually made it unnecessary.
the working conditions of the children who were employed in the Massachusetts textile mills before the age law passed.
the career of a factory inspector whose accuracy was recognised in her own lifetime.
the history of compulsory birth registration across the United States.

why.A: The passage sets up the affidavit as the wrong instrument for the job, gives Farrow’s diagnosis of why, and then shows the problem dissolving when registries arrived for entirely different reasons.
why.B: The mills are the setting. The passage never describes what the work was like, only how the children’s ages were established.
why.C: The accuracy is established in the final paragraph, and the passage is explicit that it is read for now, not something she was recognised for then.
why.D: Registration appears only in the single paragraph explaining why it spread, and only as it bears on the age question.

context: According to the passage, the law Farrow enforced permitted an employer to establish a child’s age by producing:

choices.text: an affidavit from a parent.
a birth certificate issued by the state.
the inspector’s written judgment.
a physician’s examination.

why.A: The first paragraph says the law "permitted an employer to satisfy an inspector with an affidavit from a parent".
why.B: The passage says most of these families had no certificate, which is the whole reason the affidavit existed.
why.C: Farrow recorded her judgment in a second column of her own, not as something the law recognized.
why.D: No physician appears anywhere in the passage.

context: The passage suggests that a mother who swore to an inaccurate age most often did so because she:

choices.text: did not know the date and gave a figure she had reason to think was close enough.
had been told what to say by the management of the mill that wanted the child.
was concealing a birth certificate the family had all along.
expected that nobody would ever check her sworn figure against a record.

why.A: The second paragraph says a mother asked to swear "often did not know it", and would give an age she "had every reason to believe was close enough".
why.B: No pressure from employers is described. Farrow’s account locates the problem in the record, not in coercion.
why.C: The passage says many families had no certificate at all, so there was usually nothing to conceal.
why.D: There was no record to check against, which is the point — not that checking was being evaded.

context: Farrow’s 1913 memorandum implies that she regarded false swearing as:

choices.text: a symptom of a recording failure rather than the underlying problem.
the most serious offense an inspector was likely to encounter.
impossible to detect without a physician’s help.
less common than other inspectors believed it to be.

why.A: Her proposed remedy was a registry rather than a stiffer penalty for false swearing, which only makes sense if she thought the swearing was downstream of the missing record.
why.B: Treating it as the gravest offense would have pointed her toward penalties, which is the remedy she specifically did not propose.
why.C: She judged ages herself, without a physician, and did so accurately.
why.D: She reports disagreement in more than two visits in three, which is a high rate, not a low one.

context: The fourth paragraph functions primarily to:

choices.text: show that the remedy Farrow wanted arrived for reasons that had nothing to do with her argument.
describe the actuarial methods the insurance industry was developing in those same years.
establish the date on which Farrow finally left the inspectorate.
contrast conditions in the northeast with conditions in the rest of the country.

why.A: It lists pensions, the draft and insurance as the motives, and then says outright that the question stopped "not because anyone won the argument".
why.B: The actuarial tables are named in a single clause as one motive among three, and are never described.
why.C: Her departure in 1919 belongs to the following paragraph, not to this one.
why.D: The northeast is mentioned once to bound a claim about coverage, not to set up a regional comparison.

context: The passage is organized as:

choices.text: a problem, one official’s diagnosis of it, and the unrelated development that dissolved it.
a chronological biography of a single public official and the office she worked in.
a comparison of two competing pieces of legislation and their effects.
a summary of the evidence followed by a rebuttal of that evidence.

why.A: The gap between the two columns is the problem, the 1913 memorandum is the diagnosis, and the registry paragraph is the development that ends the problem without resolving the argument.
why.B: A biography would not end with the subject "difficult to follow" and her ledgers read for a purpose she did not intend.
why.C: Only one law is described, and the registry is not presented as a rival piece of legislation.
why.D: Nothing in the passage is rebutted. The final paragraph adds a finding rather than answering one.

context: The author’s attitude toward Farrow is best described as:

choices.text: respectful of her reasoning and candid about how little effect it had.
admiring of her achievements and confident that they were recognized.
skeptical of the accuracy she is now credited with.
detached, treating her as one example among many.

why.A: Her notes are called careful and her judgments accurate, and the passage still says the memorandum "was not acted on" and that no one won the argument.
why.B: The passage says the opposite about recognition — she is difficult to follow after 1919, and the ledgers are read for something she was not trying to show.
why.C: The eighty-percent figure is reported without hedging, and the author raises no doubt about it.
why.D: She is the only person the passage follows, and her reasoning is set out at length.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that Farrow’s judgments of age were reliable?

choices.text: Her judged ages matched certificates issued later within a year about eighty percent of the time.
She kept forty-one ledgers over the course of a career that ran from the passage of the law to 1919.
Her 1913 memorandum circulated widely among the other inspectors.
She told a state commission that what she looked at was the hands.

why.A: This is a check of her judgments against an independent record made afterward, which is what evidence of accuracy has to be.
why.B: The number of ledgers shows how much she recorded, not whether what she recorded was right.
why.C: Circulation shows her argument was read, which is a separate matter from her accuracy.
why.D: That remark describes her method, or rather her inability to describe it, and establishes nothing about the results.

context: As used in the final paragraph, "follow" most nearly means:

choices.text: trace the later course of.
obey.
understand.
come after in sequence.

why.A: The sentence concerns what became of Farrow after 1919, so following her means tracking where she went.
why.B: Obeying would require an instruction, and nothing in the sentence issues one.
why.C: The difficulty is in locating her afterward, not in making sense of her.
why.D: That sense needs two things in an order, and the sentence names only Farrow.

context: The passage draws its central distinction between:

choices.text: certifying a fact and having recorded that fact in the first place.
the reach of state law and that of municipal ordinance.
the authority of an inspector and the authority of an employer.
conditions in the northeast and those in the rest of the country.

why.A: Farrow’s argument is that the affidavit "asked a parent to certify a fact the state had never bothered to record" — the certifying and the recording are precisely what the passage separates.
why.B: The passage mentions the city and the states but never sets their laws against each other.
why.C: The affidavit is what the employer produces and the inspector accepts, so the two are not in conflict over authority.
why.D: The one regional reference bounds a claim about coverage and is never developed into a contrast.

context: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.text: a decision about what to uncover in a layered panel, and the competing principles behind it.
the technical methods that conservators use to image a panel like this one without damaging it.
the attribution of the Nativity on this panel to a follower of Gerard David.
the practice of overpainting an older panel in sixteenth-century workshops.

why.A: The discovery opens the passage, two opposed positions occupy its middle, and the department’s decision and its justification close it.
why.B: Infrared and X-ray appear once, as the form the published record took, and are never explained.
why.C: The attribution is given in the first paragraph as background and is never argued about.
why.D: Overpainting appears only inside the second position’s argument, as a reason the top layer is itself a restoration.

context: According to the passage, the layer found directly on the bare oak was:

choices.text: a drawing.
a ground with no image on it.
an earlier Nativity.
the 1520 Nativity.

why.A: The first paragraph works downward and ends "on the bare oak, a drawing".
why.B: The blank ground is the layer immediately above the drawing, not the one on the wood.
why.C: The earlier Nativity is the second layer from the top.
why.D: The 1520 Nativity is the visible surface, the layer furthest from the oak.

context: The second position would most likely object to the first position on the grounds that it:

choices.text: grants authority to the topmost layer without any reason beyond its being topmost.
underestimates how difficult it actually is to remove a whole layer of old paint cleanly.
assumes the lower paintings must be of higher artistic quality.
disregards the costume evidence that was used to date the panel.

why.A: The fourth paragraph puts this as a question: why should the last hand to touch a panel have more authority than the first? That is an objection to the rule, not to the painting.
why.B: Technical difficulty is never raised by either position.
why.C: The passage says explicitly that the second position "does not hold that older is better".
why.D: The costume dating is stated once as background, and neither position disputes it.

context: The statement that the drawing on the oak "was never meant to be seen" serves to:

choices.text: support the first position’s view that not everything beneath a surface belongs to the finished work.
explain why infrared imaging was needed before anyone could find it.
establish that the drawing on the oak came from a different hand than either of the paintings above it.
cast doubt on the attribution of the panel to a follower of Gerard David.

why.A: It closes the paragraph setting out the first position, and it does the work of distinguishing the finished object from the working notes underneath it.
why.B: The imaging is described two paragraphs later and introduced for a different reason.
why.C: The passage never says who made the drawing, only that it was not meant to be seen.
why.D: The attribution concerns the top layer, and this sentence is about the oak beneath everything.

context: The passage is organized as:

choices.text: a discovery, two opposed positions on what to do about it, and the resolution actually adopted.
a chronological account of one restoration project, followed from its start through to its finish.
a general principle illustrated through a series of comparable cases.
an argument for one of the positions and a rebuttal of the other.

why.A: Paragraph one is the discovery, paragraphs three and four are the two positions, and the last two give the decision and the conservator’s account of it.
why.B: The passage skips most of the project and spends its length on an argument rather than a sequence of events.
why.C: Only one case is discussed. The author says the argument recurs but gives no other instance.
why.D: The author argues for neither position and says the decision satisfied neither.

context: The author’s treatment of the second position is best described as:

choices.text: deliberately even-handed, noting that it is usually presented less carefully than it deserves.
dismissive, treating the position as nothing more than a caricature of a serious view.
enthusiastic, endorsing the position over the first one.
so neutral that the position itself is never actually stated.

why.A: The paragraph opens by saying the position "is less easily caricatured than it is usually made to sound", and then states it carefully — the remark is a correction of how it is usually handled.
why.B: The author names the caricature in order to set it aside, which is the opposite of endorsing it.
why.C: The passage gives the first position an equally careful hearing and endorses neither.
why.D: The position is stated at length, including the question it rests on.

context: Which statement best supports the senior conservator’s claim that the decision was not a compromise?

choices.text: The department decided the panel’s worth as an object and its worth as evidence were separate questions, only one needing paint removed.
The decision the department finally adopted satisfied neither of the two positions that had been argued for two years.
The argument occupied the whole department for two years before any decision about the panel was reached at all.
The imaging of every one of the layers was published at full resolution as a permanent record rather than merely as catalogue illustrations.

why.A: Her definition is that a compromise splits a difference. Separating two values and answering each on its own terms is not splitting anything, which is why she refuses the word.
why.B: Satisfying neither side is what a compromise usually looks like, so this points the other way.
why.C: How long the argument took says nothing about the shape of its conclusion.
why.D: How thorough the record is says nothing about why the decision itself was principled.

context: As used in the fourth paragraph, "authoritative" most nearly means:

choices.text: entitled to be treated as the definitive version.
issued by an officially constituted body.
commanding in manner or in appearance.
enforced strictly and consistently wherever it applies.

why.A: The sentence asks why the topmost layer should count as the painting, so the word is about which version has the final claim.
why.B: No official body issued any layer of the panel; the question is which layer is the painting.
why.C: That sense describes a person’s bearing, and the subject here is a layer of paint.
why.D: Enforcement belongs to rules, and the passage is asking which object counts as the work.

context: It can reasonably be inferred that the published images allow the lower paintings to be:

choices.text: studied in detail even though they will remain covered.
hung where visitors could see them alongside the 1520 Nativity.
dated rather more precisely than the visible surface.
removed and remounted onto separate panels.

why.A: The passage says the lower paintings "can be studied by anyone, and will never be seen", which is only possible because the record exists apart from the object.
why.B: They remain under the paint. What hangs in the gallery is still the 1520 Nativity.
why.C: No dates are given for the lower layers at all, so nothing could be compared.
why.D: Removing them is precisely what the department decided against doing.

context: The two positions described in the passage differ most fundamentally over:

choices.text: what gives one layer of a panel a better claim than another to be the work itself.
whether the lower layers are worth documenting at all before they disappear from view again.
how much weight the costume evidence should carry in dating the panel.
whether removing an upper layer is technically achievable at all.

why.A: The first position takes the last coherent state; the second asks why last should mean authoritative. Both are answers to the same question about which layer counts.
why.B: The first position calls the lower layers "worth recording, worth publishing", so documentation is common ground.
why.C: Neither position raises the costume dating, which appears only as background.
why.D: Both assume removal is possible — the first objects that it would destroy the visible painting, which presupposes it could be done.

context: The passage as a whole is organised as:

choices.text: an attractive inference, a long test of it, and a narrowing of what it supports.
a chronological account of one bleaching event and the damage that it caused.
a comparison of two competing explanations for a decline in reef fish counts.
a defence of acoustic monitoring against critics who would abandon the method.

why.A: Correct — the first paragraph states the inference, the middle paragraphs test it over nine years, and the last two say what survives.
why.B: The bleaching is mentioned once, in a single clause, as the starting condition rather than as the subject.
why.C: Only one explanation of the divergence is offered, and no competing account of fish counts appears anywhere.
why.D: No critic is named or answered; the narrowing comes from Baptista, who still uses the method herself.

context: The paragraph reporting that the records came apart functions in the passage as:

choices.text: a summary of everything the nine years of recordings established.
the break in the agreement the previous paragraph had just described.
the first mention of the closure the local cooperative put in place.
the explanation of why shrimp noise falls as coral cover keeps rising.

why.A: It covers three years of a nine-year record and summarises nothing that came before it.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph before it reports four years of agreement, and this one is where that agreement ends.
why.C: The closure is introduced two paragraphs earlier, in the account of how the study was set up.
why.D: This paragraph reports the divergence; the explanation of it does not arrive until the paragraph after.

context: Baptista’s attitude toward acoustic monitoring by the end of the passage is best described as:

choices.text: confidence that loudness tracks reef health better than diver surveys do.
indifference as to which of the two records a reef manager relies on.
continued use of it, paired with a narrower claim about what it measures.
regret at nine years spent on a method that turned out to have failed.

why.A: That was her 2017 position, and the passage exists to record how she left it behind.
why.B: The last paragraph turns on the difference between the two records, which is the opposite of indifference.
why.C: Correct — she still records and would rather have the hydrophone, but says loudness was never a measure of health.
why.D: She says explicitly that the method is not useless, and she has not stopped using it.

context: The remark that the explanation "turned out to be uninteresting in the way that correct explanations often are" conveys:

choices.text: impatience with Baptista for needing two more years to find it.
doubt about whether the explanation offered is in fact the right one.
enthusiasm for the novelty of what the shrimp turned out to be doing.
a dry acceptance that the true account is rarely the dramatic one.

why.A: The two years are reported without objection, and the sentence faults the explanation for nothing.
why.B: The word "correct" is doing the opposite work: it grants the explanation before calling it dull.
why.C: Nothing here is presented as novel; the point is that the answer was ordinary.
why.D: Correct — calling correctness routinely uninteresting is a wry concession, not a complaint about this case.

context: Which finding most directly supports the claim that loudness measured housing rather than health?

choices.text: Coral growth slowly cemented over the rubble the snapping shrimp had occupied.
Coral cover on the bank rose from nine percent to twenty-two in four years.
The sound record moved earlier than the twice-yearly diver surveys did.
The reef lost nearly six decibels in the band where the snapping shrimp sit.

why.A: Correct — it names the mechanism: the noise fell because the cavities the noisy animals live in were closing up.
why.B: Rising coral cover is the recovery itself, and on its own it says nothing about what the sound was tracking.
why.C: Moving earlier was the reason to prefer the sound record, not evidence about what it measured.
why.D: The decibel drop is the puzzle the claim has to explain; by itself it does not explain anything.

context: The observation about what the cooperative would have concluded in 2019 is offered mainly to show that:

choices.text: sound records are cheaper to collect than repeated diver transects are.
a mismeasured index can recommend abandoning the thing that is working.
the cooperative lacked the training needed to read a hydrophone record.
the closure should have been lifted in 2019 and then imposed again later.

why.A: The cost advantage is granted earlier and is not what this final observation turns on.
why.B: Correct — the sound record would have condemned the closure in the years the closure was in fact succeeding.
why.C: The point is not that the cooperative would have misread the record but that the record itself misled.
why.D: The passage says the closure worked, so it recommends nothing of the kind.

context: As it is used in the first paragraph, the word "short" in "The inference was short and attractive" most nearly means:

choices.text: lacking in courtesy.
below a required amount.
reached in few steps.
lasting only briefly.

why.A: That sense applies to a manner of speaking to someone, and no speaker is being described.
why.B: Nothing is being measured against a requirement here, which is what that sense needs.
why.C: Correct — the next sentence lays out the inference in three clauses, showing how little reasoning it takes.
why.D: The inference held for years and is still current, so brevity in time is not the sense.

context: As it is used in the fourth paragraph, the word "sensitive" most nearly means:

choices.text: easily upset by criticism.
needing to be handled with care.
responsive to physical touch.
quicker to register a change.

why.A: That sense applies to people, and the thing called sensitive here is a record of measurements.
why.B: Careful handling is not at issue; the sentence is comparing how soon each record moved.
why.C: A hydrophone record is not touched at all, and the comparison is about timing rather than contact.
why.D: Correct — the colon that follows explains it: the sound record moved earlier than the surveys did.

context: The comparison to "frying bacon" in the first paragraph serves mainly to:

choices.text: give a reader who has never heard a reef something familiar to hold onto.
suggest that the noise of a reef is unpleasant to listen to for very long.
establish that snapping shrimp are the loudest animals living on the bank.
contrast the sound of this reef with the silence of a badly damaged one.

why.A: Correct — it translates an unfamiliar underwater sound into one almost any reader has stood next to.
why.B: No judgement about the noise being unpleasant appears anywhere in the paragraph.
why.C: The shrimp are one of three sources listed, and their loudness relative to the others is not raised until later.
why.D: Damaged reefs come up two sentences later, and the bacon is offered before any contrast is drawn.

context: The passage most strongly suggests that an index of this kind is most dangerous when it:

choices.text: disagrees with every other record from the first year it is collected.
agrees with the thing it stands for long enough to be trusted on its own.
costs more to collect than the survey it was meant to stand in for does.
is collected by a local cooperative rather than by trained divers.

why.A: An index that never agrees with anything would be discarded early, which is the safe case rather than the dangerous one.
why.B: Correct — four years of agreement are what earned the sound record its authority, and it kept that authority after the agreement ended.
why.C: Cost is presented as the sound record’s advantage, and the passage never treats expense as a hazard.
why.D: The cooperative managed the closure; it did not collect either record, and no such contrast is drawn.

context: Which of the following best describes the way the passage is put together?

choices.text: a standard measure, a second one run beside it, and what their disagreement shows.
a history of how the state’s library funding formula came to be written.
an argument that circulation should be dropped as a measure of library use.
a profile of one director and the five branches she has run since 2014.

why.A: Correct — circulation opens the passage, the sweep joins it, and the closing paragraphs read the gap.
why.B: The formula is mentioned twice but never traced back to who wrote it or when.
why.C: The sixth paragraph says plainly that circulation is not a bad measure, only a partial one.
why.D: Adeyemi-Lowe arrives in the fifth paragraph, and the branches are counted once in passing.

context: The short third paragraph functions in the passage chiefly to:

choices.text: establish that Kettleman runs a main branch and four smaller ones.
separate the method, which is common, from the record, which is not.
explain the fixed schedule on which staff walk the library floor.
introduce the disagreement between the two records for the first time.

why.A: The branches are counted in the second paragraph, and nothing here returns to them.
why.B: Correct — it grants that sweeps are ordinary, so the claim has to rest on nine published years.
why.C: The schedule is given in the paragraph before, as part of describing what the sweep is.
why.D: The disagreement arrives in the paragraph after this one, which reports it collection by collection.

context: The fourth paragraph differs from the paragraphs before it chiefly in that it:

choices.text: concedes that the sweep cannot show whether anybody read anything.
explains why an atlas is borrowed less often than a popular novel.
reports what the two records did rather than how they were collected.
names the director of the Kettleman County system for the first time.

why.A: That concession is made by Adeyemi-Lowe later, not by the paragraph reporting the counts.
why.B: The reasons behind the gap, the atlas included, arrive two paragraphs further on.
why.C: Correct — the earlier paragraphs set the two counts up, and this is the first to put numbers beside each other.
why.D: Adeyemi-Lowe is named in the fifth paragraph, the one immediately after this.

context: Adeyemi-Lowe’s attitude toward circulation as a measure is best described as:

choices.text: frustration at a formula she has spent nine years trying to overturn.
confidence that the sweep should replace it as the number reported.
indifference to which of the two numbers the state chooses to use.
acceptance of what it counts, paired with insistence on what it does not.

why.A: She never asks for the formula to change; she asks that the note beside it be read.
why.B: She says the sweep does not show that anybody read anything, which is no case for replacing.
why.C: She spent six years on the wording of the note, which is the opposite of not caring.
why.D: Correct — she says circulation is not a bad measure, only one that counts a single behaviour.

context: The remark that Adeyemi-Lowe is "careful not to overclaim" serves mainly to:

choices.text: mark the limit she sets before she draws anything from the sweep.
suggest that she doubts the sweep counts were recorded accurately.
criticise other librarians who have claimed too much for the method.
signal that the writer disagrees with the conclusion she reaches.

why.A: Correct — the sentence after it says what the sweep does not show before saying what it does.
why.B: Her caution is about what the counts mean, not about whether they were taken correctly.
why.C: No other librarian appears in the passage, and the method is described as ordinary practice.
why.D: The writer reports her conclusion without objection and gives it the final paragraph.

context: The final sentence of the passage conveys:

choices.text: pride in the length of the record the county has kept.
a wry sense that the hardest part of the work was the smallest.
regret that six years of effort produced only a short note.
anger at readers who will not read a longer explanation.

why.A: The nine years are mentioned earlier and without emphasis, and this sentence is about the note.
why.B: Correct — she calls the note the part that matters, then reports how long it took to shorten it.
why.C: She names the note as the thing that matters, so the six years are not presented as wasted.
why.D: The sentence faults nobody; it treats a short note as the goal rather than as a surrender.

context: Which finding most directly supports the claim that circulation misses work a collection is doing?

choices.text: Reference material was once kept non-circulating as a matter of policy.
The state has not changed the formula it uses to fund the system.
A shelf that circulated eleven times in a year drew 2,300 sweep entries.
Popular fiction rises and falls in both records at the same time.

why.A: The old policy helps explain the habit, but it is not itself a measurement of use.
why.B: What the state does with the numbers is not evidence about what the numbers capture.
why.C: Correct — the same shelf is nearly invisible in one record and heavily used in the other.
why.D: Fiction is the collection where the two agree, so it shows the measure working, not failing.

context: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the case Kettleman makes for the sweep?

choices.text: The sweep was carried out four times a day rather than continuously.
Other library systems in the state have run sweeps of their own.
Local history is the smallest collection the main branch holds.
Most items recorded in a sweep were set down by staff reshelving carts.

why.A: The schedule is stated in the passage, and a fixed interval is what makes the counts comparable.
why.B: The passage says the method is ordinary, so other systems running it changes nothing.
why.C: Collection size would not explain one shelf appearing 2,300 times in the sweep record.
why.D: Correct — the sweep is meant to count what a person took off a shelf, and this makes it count staff.

context: The passage draws which contrast between popular fiction and local history?

choices.text: The two records agree about one and come apart completely about the other.
One is borrowed by adults and the other chiefly by students doing research.
One was placed on a withdrawal list in 2016 and the other was not.
One is counted in the sweep and the other is counted in circulation.

why.A: Correct — fiction rises and falls in both counts together, while local history splits them apart.
why.B: The passage never says who borrows either collection or what they are doing with it.
why.C: The withdrawal list is mentioned for local history, but fiction is never weighed against it.
why.D: Both collections appear in both records, which is what makes the comparison possible at all.

context: As used in the sixth paragraph, "consulted" most nearly means:

choices.text: compared against another source.
looked into for one particular thing.
asked for advice or an opinion.
borrowed for use at home.

why.A: Nothing in the paragraph involves setting one source beside another to check it.
why.B: Correct — the sentence sets it against reading through, so it means dipping in for a single item.
why.C: That is the sense the word carries about a person, and a yearbook is not being asked anything.
why.D: Taking a thing home is exactly the behaviour the paragraph says a yearbook does not attract.

context: The comparison of the school violin to "a bad microphone" serves to convey that it:

choices.text: reduced good and bad playing alike to the same pleasant sound.
produced a harsh sound that was unpleasant to listen to.
was too quiet to be heard from the back of a hall.
had been repaired badly at some point in its history.

why.A: Correct — the sentence says it flattened everything into the same pleasant nothing.
why.B: The complaint runs the other way: the school violin was too pleasant, not harsh.
why.C: Volume is never mentioned, and the comparison is about what the instrument reported.
why.D: The repaired crack belongs to the Saxony violin, not to the school instrument.

context: In saying that the Saxony violin "reported", the narrator means that it:

choices.text: made a mechanical noise that interfered with the music.
returned an honest account of what the player had actually done.
was loud enough to carry over the rest of the orchestra.
had been described in writing by the teacher who lent it.

why.A: The scrape comes from the narrator’s bowing, not from a fault in the instrument.
why.B: Correct — the sentence after it gives the example: a crooked bow comes back as an audible scrape.
why.C: Nothing in the passage concerns how far the instrument could be heard.
why.D: The word describes what the violin did to the narrator’s playing, not what anyone wrote down.

context: The passage contrasts the school violin with the Saxony violin chiefly in terms of:

choices.text: how much each of the two was worth to a collector.
the number of years the narrator played each one.
how much of the player’s error each one passed on.
the countries in which each of them was built.

why.A: The passage says outright that the Saxony violin was not valuable, so value is not the contrast.
why.B: Four years and eighteen months are both given, but neither is weighed against the other.
why.C: Correct — one flattened everything into pleasant nothing and the other returned a crooked bow.
why.D: Saxony is named once for the loan violin, and the school instrument’s origin never comes up.

context: The two halves of Mr. Vasiliou’s lesson differ in that the second half concerns:

choices.text: the repaired crack that softened the violin’s low notes.
the eighteen months for which the violin was lent.
how much the narrator’s playing improved that autumn.
what his own silence over four years had been for.

why.A: The crack is a physical detail of the instrument and no part of what he was teaching.
why.B: The length of the loan belongs to the first thing he said, which the narrator heard at once.
why.C: The autumn is where the narrator finds the problem, not where the second half of the lesson lies.
why.D: Correct — the last paragraph says he had heard what the school violin was hiding and never said so.

context: The fifth paragraph functions in the passage chiefly to:

choices.text: name what the new instrument had exposed in the narrator’s playing.
describe the physical condition of the violin that was lent.
explain why Mr. Vasiliou set the loan at eighteen months.
introduce the teacher who had taught the narrator for four years.

why.A: Correct — it turns "unplayable by me" into a specific charge: the playing had been a kind of rounding.
why.B: The crack and the soft low notes are given in the third paragraph, not in this one.
why.C: The passage never explains the choice of eighteen months, only that it was the term set.
why.D: Mr. Vasiliou is introduced in the opening paragraph and does not return until the last one.

context: The repetition of the phrase "the first half" in the final paragraph works to:

choices.text: show that the narrator has finally understood the whole lesson.
mark that the narrator has made the same mistake a second time.
remind the reader how long the loan of the violin lasted.
suggest that the teacher had forgotten his earlier wording.

why.A: Understanding arrives a year later; the phrase marks the moment he has still not got there.
why.B: Correct — at sixteen he heard only the first half, and at eighteen he answered with it again.
why.C: The eighteen months are stated plainly elsewhere and are not what the phrase is tracking.
why.D: The teacher uses the phrase deliberately, and "again" shows he remembers it exactly.

context: The passage as a whole is best described as an account of:

choices.text: the difficulty of repairing a crack beneath the bass bar.
a teacher’s decision to stop giving lessons to a student.
what an honest instrument revealed, and how long the lesson took.
the history of a factory violin built somewhere in Saxony.

why.A: The crack explains a quirk in damp weather and is never the subject of the passage.
why.B: The lessons end only because the narrator grows up; no decision to stop them is described.
why.C: Correct — the loan, the autumn of discovery and the further year are stages of a single lesson.
why.D: Saxony is a guess in one clause, and the passage tells no history of the instrument.

context: The narrator’s attitude toward Mr. Vasiliou by the end of the passage is best described as:

choices.text: resentment at four years of criticism that was never spoken.
amusement at a teacher who spoke mostly in riddles.
regret that the loan was not made several years earlier.
recognition of a patience the narrator could not see at the time.

why.A: The point of that sentence is that the criticism was held back on purpose and for the student.
why.B: The two halves are a teaching device, and the narrator treats them seriously rather than lightly.
why.C: The narrator never suggests the timing was wrong; the waiting is what the ending credits.
why.D: Correct — the closing sentence explains the silence as waiting rather than as withholding.

context: As used in the fifth paragraph, "rounding" most nearly means:

choices.text: smoothing a value to something near enough.
moving in a circular path around a point.
gathering scattered things into one place.
making an edge or a corner less sharp.

why.A: Correct — the next sentence says he had been close enough for an instrument that could not tell.
why.B: The geometric sense has nothing to do with intonation or with the sentences around it.
why.C: Nothing is being collected; the paragraph is about accuracy rather than about gathering.
why.D: The literal sense of softening an edge does not fit a claim about being in tune.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that the Saxony violin was the more honest of the two?

choices.text: Beside the school instruments it looked like a brown coat among black.
A bow drawn slightly crooked came back as a scrape the narrator could hear.
The violin arrived in a cardboard box lined with a wool coat.
A repaired crack made the low notes go soft in damp weather.

why.A: The brown coat describes how the violin looked, and looks are not what the claim is about.
why.B: Correct — it is the one detail showing the instrument returning an error the player had made.
why.C: The box shows how carefully Mr. Vasiliou handled it, not what it did to the playing.
why.D: Soft low notes are a fault in the instrument, which is the opposite of an honest report.

context: The passage is organized primarily as:

choices.text: a position held, abandoned for a reason, and replaced by a test.
a chronological history of museum labelling from 1608 onward.
a comparison of two museums with opposite labelling policies.
a list of the practical rules a new label writer is given.

why.A: Correct — the writer holds the silent-wall view, loses it on a Tuesday, and lands on a rule.
why.B: The date 1608 belongs to one painting; no history of the practice is traced.
why.C: Only one institution is described, and its curatorial department is not a second museum.
why.D: The one rule offered arrives at the end as a conclusion, not as instruction given to the writer.

context: The fourth paragraph functions in the passage’s structure as:

choices.text: a restatement of the opening paragraph’s point about eleven seconds.
the counterexample that breaks the position set out just before it.
the first statement of the objection the curators had raised.
a digression that has little bearing on the argument around it.

why.A: The eleven seconds return only in the last paragraph, and not as this paragraph’s point.
why.B: Correct — the third paragraph ends with the writer holding the purest position, and this ends it.
why.C: The curators’ objection is stated in the paragraph before, not in this one.
why.D: It carries the turn of the whole essay and is the reason the position changes.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the curatorial objection is best described as:

choices.text: entirely persuaded, to the point of adopting it permanently.
indifferent, since labels are written whatever the curators say.
respectful of its force while unwilling to follow it all the way.
dismissive of a complaint the writer considers merely territorial.

why.A: The writer held it for about two years and then abandoned it, so it did not last.
why.B: Indifference would not have produced two years of holding the position.
why.C: Correct — the objection is called serious and the writer once held it, but it does not survive.
why.D: Nothing frames the objection as a turf dispute; it is given a reason and taken seriously.

context: In the final paragraph the writer’s tone toward their own past work is best described as:

choices.text: bitter that the labels were never credited to the person who wrote them.
confident that the rule was kept and that most of the labels succeeded.
anxious that visitors are still being steered without knowing it.
unsentimental about the failures and quietly pleased by the few that hold.

why.A: Anonymity is raised in the paragraph before and treated as not mattering at all.
why.B: The passage says outright that most of the old labels fail the writer’s own test.
why.C: The steering worry belongs to the curators, and the ending is about the writer’s record.
why.D: Correct — "Most of them fail" is stated flatly, and the writer lingers at the two or three.

context: Which detail best supports the claim that a bare label can leave a visitor stranded?

choices.text: A man in the Dutch gallery asked whether a 1608 winter scene was a photograph.
Visitors give the picture about eleven seconds and the label about twenty.
The writer wrote labels for eleven years and signed none of them.
The purest position lists title, artist, date, medium and nothing else.

why.A: Correct — the bare label gave him the date and still left him without the language for it.
why.B: The timings show how briefly labels are read, not what a bare one fails to supply.
why.C: The length of the writer’s career says nothing about what a visitor can use.
why.D: That is the position itself; the evidence against it is what the man said.

context: The writer supports the claim that a label steers the viewer chiefly by:

choices.text: describing the training that new label writers are required to complete.
showing how three different opening words each produce a different reading.
citing a survey of visitors conducted across several Dutch galleries.
quoting the curatorial department’s written policy on wall text.

why.A: No training is described anywhere; what the job teaches comes from doing it.
why.B: Correct — date first, name first and pigment first are given as three different doors.
why.C: The eleven and twenty seconds are stated as facts, not sourced to any survey.
why.D: The curators’ objection is paraphrased in the writer’s own words, never quoted.

context: The description of a label as "a door held open at a particular angle" conveys that a label:

choices.text: can be shut by any visitor who prefers to look without reading.
is a decorative object placed beside the work for its own sake.
gives access to the work while narrowing what will be seen first.
blocks the viewer from the painting until the text has been read.

why.A: Nothing in the image belongs to the visitor; the angle is set by the writer.
why.B: The image is about what the label does to seeing, not about how it looks on the wall.
why.C: Correct — a door lets you in, and its angle decides what you face when you come through.
why.D: A held-open door is the opposite of a barrier, and the sentence contrasts it with a summary.

context: As used in the third paragraph, "forecloses" most nearly means:

choices.text: repossesses property from an owner who has not paid.
announces a conclusion in advance of the evidence.
brings an unfinished argument to an orderly close.
shuts off possibilities before they can be considered.

why.A: The financial sense has nothing to do with a sentence about wall text.
why.B: An announcement would be something the visitor hears; the loss here is unnoticed.
why.C: An orderly close suggests completion, but the objection is about what is cut off.
why.D: Correct — the sentence pairs it with steering, so the cost is the readings never reached.

context: The writer contrasts the silent wall with the chatty one in order to show that:

choices.text: the final rule belongs to neither of the two familiar positions.
the chatty wall is the safer of the two options for a museum.
both approaches were abandoned by the curatorial department.
the two approaches produce identical results for most visitors.

why.A: Correct — the sentence rejects both in turn before the looking-back test is offered.
why.B: The writer says plainly that belief in the chatty wall never started.
why.C: The curators argued for the silent wall; nothing says they gave up either view.
why.D: The whole passage rests on the two producing very different eleven seconds.

context: The main idea of the passage is that a museum label:

choices.text: ought to carry the name of the person who wrote it.
should be judged by whether it sends the visitor back to the work.
should be kept to the title, artist, date and medium alone.
matters less than the painting it is asked to sit beside.

why.A: Anonymity is mentioned twice and dismissed as not mattering at the end.
why.B: Correct — the rule the writer arrives at is the standard the last two paragraphs apply.
why.C: That is the position the writer abandons after the Tuesday in the Dutch gallery.
why.D: The passage argues the opposite: ninety words decide what a stranger notices for life.

context: The passage is organized primarily as:

choices.text: two rival explanations, the evidence between them, and what is still unsettled.
a chronological history of European robin migration studies since 1970.
a set of instructions for testing a bird’s orientation in a laboratory.
an argument that magnetic navigation in birds is not real at all.

why.A: Correct — the two candidates are set out, weighed against results, and left short of a full answer.
why.B: Fifty years of argument is mentioned once; no sequence of studies is traced by date.
why.C: Experiments are described for what they showed, never as procedures to follow.
why.D: The opening establishes that something in the bird reads the field; that is not in dispute.

context: The fifth paragraph contributes to the passage’s structure chiefly by:

choices.text: explaining why the retinal mechanism cannot account for the map sense.
removing support from the candidate the passage introduced first.
introducing a third mechanism that neither earlier paragraph considered.
restating the radio-frequency result in more accessible language.

why.A: The limits of the retinal mechanism are the closing paragraph’s business, not this one’s.
why.B: Correct — the beak cells were the mechanical candidate’s physical evidence, and they are reassigned.
why.C: No third mechanism appears; the paragraph is about what one of the two lost.
why.D: The radio-frequency result belongs to the paragraph before and is not repeated here.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the magnetite hypothesis is best described as:

choices.text: convinced that it remains the better of the two available explanations.
uninterested, since the passage is concerned only with the retina.
sympathetic to its appeal while following the evidence away from it.
contemptuous of researchers who proposed something so obviously wrong.

why.A: The passage says the weight of evidence moved toward the retina instead.
why.B: Two full paragraphs are given to it, which is not the treatment of a side issue.
why.C: Correct — it is called satisfying and concrete, and then shown losing ground twice over.
why.D: Nothing mocks anyone; the reassignment of the beak cells is reported without blame.

context: In the final paragraph the writer’s attitude toward what remains unknown is best described as:

choices.text: frustrated that fifty years has produced so little.
confident the map sense uses the same mechanism.
doubtful a displaced bird finds its way home.
untroubled by what is still open.

why.A: The argument is called unusually productive, which is the opposite of a complaint.
why.B: The paragraph raises iron-based sensing as the likelier candidate for that second job.
why.C: Displacement is offered as something birds evidently manage and nobody has explained.
why.D: Correct — the gap is stated plainly, with the honest summary preferred to the headlines.

context: Which result most directly supports locating the compass in the retina rather than the beak?

choices.text: A weak radio-frequency field, too feeble to move a crystal, scrambles orientation.
Magnetite crystals were reported in the upper beaks of several migratory species.
A robin taken from a German garden sets off toward the southwest when released.
Cryptochrome is a light-sensitive protein that sits in the retina of the bird.

why.A: Correct — it rules out a mechanical needle by being far too weak to move one.
why.B: That is the evidence for the beak, and the passage later reassigns the cells that carried it.
why.C: The southwest heading shows a magnetic sense exists without saying where it sits.
why.D: Where the protein sits is the hypothesis being tested, not a result that tests it.

context: Which finding, if established, would most weaken the case built in the fourth paragraph?

choices.text: The field is weaker over Germany than Norway.
Robins orient normally in the dark.
Cryptochrome occurs in non-migratory birds too.
Magnetite occurs in the beaks of fish as well.

why.A: Field strength varies everywhere and bears on neither result in that paragraph.
why.B: Correct — the paragraph rests on light being required, and this would remove that requirement.
why.C: A protein found more widely than expected says nothing about whether it senses the field.
why.D: Where else magnetite occurs leaves the light and radio-frequency results untouched.

context: The statement that "A compass and a map are not the same instrument" serves to distinguish:

choices.text: the mechanical hypothesis from the chemical one that displaced it.
migratory species of bird from the species that stay in one place.
knowing which way is north from knowing where you have been taken.
laboratory testing of captive birds from observation of birds in the wild.

why.A: Both candidates are compasses; the map is a separate job that neither has explained.
why.B: Non-migratory birds are not discussed, so the image cannot be drawing that line.
why.C: Correct — the next sentences give direction to the compass and displacement to the map.
why.D: Captivity and the wild are never contrasted anywhere in the passage.

context: The writer says a bird would "not feel north so much as see it" in order to convey that the retinal mechanism:

choices.text: produces a bright spot on the horizon that the bird can fly toward.
works only in daylight and shuts down completely after dusk.
requires the bird to have learned the route before it can be used.
delivers direction as part of vision rather than as a push on a nerve.

why.A: The passage describes a faint pattern laid over the view, not a point of light to aim at.
why.B: Light is needed, but the sentence is about the form of the signal rather than its schedule.
why.C: Learning is never mentioned; the robin in the first paragraph sets off without being taught.
why.D: Correct — the contrast is with the beak needle, whose signal is a physical push on a nerve.

context: As used in the final paragraph, "robustly" most nearly means:

choices.text: in a way that holds up under testing.
with unusual physical strength or vigour.
in a manner that is loud and unsubtle.
without allowing for any exception at all.

why.A: Correct — it modifies "explains", and the two results in the fourth paragraph are the testing.
why.B: Physical vigour belongs to bodies rather than to explanations.
why.C: The word describes how well the explanation survives, not how it sounds.
why.D: The same sentence goes on to name a large exception, so nothing is being claimed absolutely.

context: The two candidate mechanisms differ most importantly in that only the retinal one:

choices.text: was supported by images later reinterpreted.
needs light in order to work.
has ever been proposed for the European robin.
explains how a displaced bird knows its direction.

why.A: The reinterpreted images were the beak cells, which belong to the mechanical candidate.
why.B: Correct — the light and colour results are the ones a mechanical needle would not care about.
why.C: Both candidates are discussed in connection with the robin from the opening paragraph.
why.D: Neither explains the map sense; that is the gap the passage closes on.

context: The passage is organized primarily as:

choices.text: a contrast between two habits, a striking result, and a limit on what it shows.
a chronological account of how jury procedure changed over the last century.
a set of recommendations for how a jury foreperson ought to run a room.
an argument that juries should be replaced by panels of trained judges.

why.A: Correct — the two room types, the first-ballot result, and the mock-jury caution, in that order.
why.B: No dates are given and no change in procedure over time is described anywhere.
why.C: The passage describes what rooms do; it never tells a foreperson what to do.
why.D: Judges are not mentioned, and nothing proposes replacing the jury with anything.

context: The fourth paragraph functions in the passage’s structure chiefly as:

choices.text: a summary of the two habits introduced at the opening.
a limit placed on the claim the passage has just made.
the first description of what an evidence-driven room does.
a second piece of evidence for the first-ballot finding.

why.A: Nothing is restated here, and the two habits are not the paragraph’s subject.
why.B: Correct — it names the closed-door problem and the mock juries the findings rest on.
why.C: The evidence-driven room is described in the second paragraph, not in this one.
why.D: It supplies no new support; it questions the footing of what has already been said.

context: The writer’s attitude toward the first-ballot finding is best described as:

choices.text: certain that it settles who is convicted and who is not.
indifferent, since the studies were all done on volunteers.
persuaded but careful about how far it reaches.
sceptical that any pattern in the data is real at all.

why.A: The closing sentence says exactly the opposite about who goes to prison.
why.B: The volunteers are raised as a caution the writer takes seriously rather than ignores.
why.C: Correct — the finding is called striking and then explicitly held back from the courtroom.
why.D: The passage says the pattern survives decades and countries, which is not scepticism.

context: The phrase "a caution that is easy to skip" suggests the writer regards the mock-jury problem as:

choices.text: so severe that the research cannot be used for anything.
a complaint raised only by people hostile to the research.
already solved by the volume of studies that have been run.
a real point that readers pass over.

why.A: The next paragraph opens by saying the caution does not dissolve the finding.
why.B: The writer raises it personally and treats it as a fair point rather than an attack.
why.C: Volume makes an artefact less likely but leaves the closed-door problem in place.
why.D: Correct — something easy to skip is something readers pass over, which is why it is flagged.

context: Which detail most directly supports the claim that an evidence-driven room serves its members better?

choices.text: Its members are less likely to report having gone along with something.
It postpones any count until the talking through the witnesses has run its course.
It is the habit that the researchers studying deliberation describe second.
Its discussion is organised around the two camps that the first poll creates.

why.A: Correct — it names an outcome for the people in the room rather than a feature of the method.
why.B: Postponing the count is what the habit is, not evidence that the habit does any good.
why.C: The order in which the two are introduced carries no claim about either one.
why.D: Camps formed by an early poll belong to the verdict-driven room instead.

context: The writer’s chief reason for not dismissing the mock-jury research is that its central pattern:

choices.text: has never once been challenged by anyone working in the field.
reappears across decades, countries and formats.
has been confirmed by observers sitting in on real deliberations.
agrees with what jurors themselves say about their own rooms.

why.A: The passage raises a challenge itself, so the research is plainly not unchallenged.
why.B: Correct — the passage says a result surviving that much variation is rarely an artefact.
why.C: Real deliberations are closed, which is the whole reason the caution exists.
why.D: Only one report from members is mentioned, and it is an outcome rather than a check.

context: The contrast between a window opening and "a door closing" conveys that an early ballot:

choices.text: makes the deliberation take considerably longer to finish.
is required by the rules under which a jury must operate.
shuts off the thinking it appears to reveal.
lets the rest of the room see what each member believes.

why.A: The verdict-driven room is described as the one that finishes sooner.
why.B: The opening paragraph says nobody instructs the room to take the vote at all.
why.C: Correct — the next sentence says the discussion afterward becomes a defence, not an enquiry.
why.D: That is the window the image rejects; the passage says the ballot is the other thing.

context: As used in the final paragraph, "artefact" most nearly means:

choices.text: an object recovered from a site and kept for study.
a deliberate attempt to mislead a reader about data.
a skilled piece of work made by hand rather than machine.
a result produced by the method rather than the world.

why.A: The archaeological sense has nothing to do with a statistical result.
why.B: Nothing suggests deception; the worry is that the setup produced the pattern by itself.
why.C: Handmade craft is a third unrelated sense of the word entirely.
why.D: Correct — the sentence contrasts it with a pattern that survives changes in the laboratory setup.

context: The two kinds of room differ most importantly in that only the evidence-driven one:

choices.text: waits before it counts a single hand.
is made up of twelve people shown into a room together.
reaches a verdict that matches its first-ballot majority.
has been studied by researchers using volunteers as jurors.

why.A: Correct — the early poll is exactly what separates the verdict-driven room from it.
why.B: Both rooms are the same twelve people; the difference is what they do first.
why.C: Finishing where the first ballot started is the verdict-driven room’s pattern.
why.D: The mock-jury method covers both habits, since both are observed in the same studies.

context: The main idea of the passage is that:

choices.text: the number of jurors in a room matters more than the order in which they speak.
when a room votes changes what it remembers, though not provably who it convicts.
juries reach the wrong verdict whenever they take a ballot in the first ten minutes.
research on deliberation is too compromised by its methods to be worth attending to.

why.A: The number twelve appears once as a setting and is never compared with anything.
why.B: Correct — the closing paragraph draws exactly that line between what is shown and what is not.
why.C: No verdict is called wrong anywhere; the passage is about memory and participation.
why.D: The caution is raised and then answered by the pattern surviving across decades.
